ideas.th: 800G+ transceiver volumes doubling and 1.6T mix lift TIA/driver ASPs; $10 EPS power vs ~$6 consensus with cellular divestiture lifting margins.
ideas.cat: Cellular module divestiture; CopperEdge hyperscaler deployment
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Semtech as a long.

Semtech is a diversified supplier of analog mixed-signal components. Approximately 35% of the business is related to signal integrity (housing its high-growth FiberEdge, CopperEdge business). Another 35% lies within its protection, sensing, and wireless products. The remaining 30% is related to various IoT assets. The presenter believes you will see significant upside from that signal integrity business that houses the fiber and connectivity solutions. First, within signal integrity, Semtech holds assets utilized in transceivers, such as TIAs and drivers. Semtech should benefit materially from the upcoming transceiver cycle. First, the overall volume of high-speed transceivers should see significant growth. The presenter thinks the market is coming from a base of 80 to 90 million 800 G and up transceivers this year to 160 to 180 million in 800 G next year—so that is roughly a double in terms of volume. The second part is, within that mix, you have more products shifting to the next-generation 1.6T transceivers. The presenter believes those next-generation transceivers can offer ASPs up to 50% to 100% higher versus the 800-gig generation for their TIA products. Within the transceiver mix specifically, the presenter expects 1.6T volume to grow from approximately 20% of the mix to just under 50%, which offers pricing upside.

And on top of that, in the next generation, Semtech should maintain strong share. Along with the organic growth as well, they made a recent acquisition of HieFo, which expands their SAM within the transceiver module market and gives them assets and a roadmap to attack the emerging NPO/CPO opportunities.

Outside of the FiberEdge business, you also can look at the copper assets. There should be growth within their linear equalizer business, which is utilized to extend the reach of copper cables. Semtech's products should be deployed by a major hyperscaler—presumably Google—and there is further upside if Nvidia utilizes this technology in future improvement designs. They are also in negotiations with other partners, so it remains to be seen how that business progresses.

Outside of this broader connectivity portfolio, Semtech is also in the process of realigning its product portfolio, and they are in the end stages of divesting this cellular module business. The presenter believes this could likely add a few hundred basis points to gross margin. So as the mix shifts to more of the signal integrity business, you have a pathway to go from a high-50%s gross margin to mid-60%s longer term.

Net-net, while supply constraints remain a key risk for this industry, the presenter sees a pathway for signal integrity to roughly double versus what consensus is currently modeling. The presenter is underwriting $10 of EPS power in a few years as consensus is closer to $6. Even applying a low-20s multiple, which is slightly below their historical average but slightly above broader networking peers, you get to approximately 60% upside from today’s stock price. And if you really dream the dream on the module, on the CopperEdge side, you can easily see the stock doubling. The presenter thinks the downside from here is likely only 25% or 30%. So they think the risk-reward skew is pretty attractive at these levels.
ideas.src: Michael Crespi <mcrespi@mchny.com> | MCH Idea Dinner Notes -- TMT -- August 10, 2026 | received 2026-08-12

ideas.th: Tower REIT at ~14x AFFO is a year from AMT-like organic growth and likely remains an M&A target for American Tower.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss SBA Communications as a long.

SBA is a communications infrastructure / tower company. It is trading at approximately 14x AFFO per share. It has an $18 billion market cap and a $35 billion EV.

From a risk-reward perspective, what the presenter is talking about as far as its multiple range—if you look at spreads versus the 10-year, it can range anywhere from 13x to 18x; so, investors are pretty optimistic on this company.

The presenter would argue that the aspect to the story that investors are not appreciating is that they are approximately a year away from having an organic growth opportunity that looks very similar to the largest tower peer in the space, American Tower, who has laid out plans for mid-single-digit top-line organic / mid-to-high-single-digits bottom-line growth. The presenter believes that SBAC is an M&A target, specifically from American Tower. The stock was trading at $170; then there were reports that it was in M&A talks and the stock subsequently traded to $210; then press reports indicated the M&A talks were over, so the stock is now trading in the high $170s. The presenter thinks those talks are likely still ongoing in some way, shape, or form.

In summary, the presenter thinks you have an attractive risk/ reward skew here. The upside on a deal is not simply the 20% to 25% you might get from multiple normalization plus positive earnings in 2028, but you also have another 25% to 50% M&A premium that could come in. Also worth noting, it is not involved at all with the AI complex, so you do not need to worry about Nvidia announcing $500 billion of financing and what that means. It should be considered a relatively safe long.
ideas.src: Michael Crespi <mcrespi@mchny.com> | MCH Idea Dinner Notes -- TMT -- August 10, 2026 | received 2026-08-12

ideas.th: Post-print US DAU selloff overdone; unique human content, ~60% revenue growth at ~12.5x EV/EBITDA, AI licensing renewals to come.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Reddit as a long.

This stock is extremely controversial. It has enormous, inordinate volatility, in the presenter's opinion. But when the presenter looks at this company, they do not see any other comparable property that has the same dimension of human content.

In terms of the setup, the stock sold off dramatically after they reported earnings on July 30th. The stock went out at $180 the night before; it was trading around $140 the next morning. So what caused the move? Their DAUs went down by approximately 200,000 in the US, while their international user growth was strong. So the fear is that user growth in the US is flattening out.

The other controversy regarding the stock is over their renewal with Google and their licensing agreement, where Google pays approximately $60 million this year, and there is talk that they were asking for $120 million. In terms of the magnitude of what Google and the other AI companies are spending on CAPEX, the renewal amount is insignificant. The presenter thinks that the overhang on the stock surrounding the renewal of the licensing agreement was blown out of proportion. Eventually, the presenter thinks there will be an agreement with Google, followed by OpenAI, and then Anthropic (because they are trying to sue them).

But what you have here is a company with 194 million shares outstanding, a $28 billion EV, that is going to generate $1.5 billion of EBITDA this year, going to $2 billion next year. You are talking 12.5 times enterprise value. There is some stock comp in there that is not insignificant, but this business has no CAPEX. Its revenue is growing 60%. It generate san enormous amount of cash flow. They bought back $250 million worth of stock in the quarter. They generate more content in one month than the entire Wikipedia library. The presenter believes that if you are Google or OpenAI, you are going to want to have access to this content. The controversy is that no one is going to go to Reddit, that they are simply going to go to Reddit via Google, and those subscribers are not as valuable. The presenter does not think that is going to happen, because there is still enormous growth internationally. Their ARPU growth is extraordinary.
ideas.src: Michael Crespi <mcrespi@mchny.com> | MCH Idea Dinner Notes -- TMT -- August 10, 2026 | received 2026-08-12

ideas.th: Vineland NJ 250MW buildout blocked by city council puts ~$2.9B of the $7-9B YE ARR target at risk while $20B+ of debt is needed.
ideas.cat: Aug 17 city council vote; 45-day appeal; Q2 earnings
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Nebius as a short.

For those not familiar with it, it is a neocloud. What is a neocloud? It depends on who you ask. They are either an NVIDIA GPU reseller, or they are a play on the future of the public cloud, where enterprises are going to be renting out dedicated GPU capacity in the same way that they do from the hyperscalers today. If the market remains significantly compute constrained long-term, these players have a place in the market.

The reason why the presenter thinks it is a short is that Nebius has a $7 to $9 billion ARR target for the end of this year. They have approximately 16 data center sites under contract, but the most critical one for this year is in Vineland, New Jersey. Vineland is going to house a Microsoft contract for them, where they will get approximately $17.4 billion over the next five years. On 300 megawatts at that site, it implies about $11.6 million of ARR per megawatt.

They have delivered 50 megawatts at that site—so 50 of the 300—and they are currently facing community backlash around being able to stand up the incremental 250 by the end of the year. A week ago, there was a city council meeting to vote on whether or not Nebius can stand up the rest of the 250, and it ended in a “no” vote. The next meeting is August 17th. Presumably, there will be another vote then. Even if that occurs, there is a 45-day appeals process, which puts you out to October 1st, if all goes well, to when they can start standing up these 250 megawatts.

The partner at the site is Bloom Energy. Bloom Energy has touted their ability to stand up 55 megawatts in 55 days for Oracle, as one of the fastest deployments they have ever done. If you do the math based on October 1st to the end of the year, it does not get to the 250 that they would need. So at $11.6 million of ARR per megawatt, the presenter believes you have $2.9 billion of that $7 to $9 billion ARR target at risk. Even if they get half of that, it is still a problem for the range, because they are assuming that it is fully stood up in the guide. So where could you be wrong? There has been some speculation that you could get a large deal announcement with Anthropic on the quarter this Wednesday. Candidly, they have two over-one-gigawatt sites that are contracted—not yet built, but contracted—that investors have been speculating that Anthropic could come in and fill. But, in the presenter’s opinion, if you ask anyone how they are modeling this business, no one puts those sites in their model without anyone filling that capacity long-term. So you need to believe that Anthropic is going to sign a meaningfully upsized deal relative to what the current market rate is on a dollars per megawatt basis.

There has also been some speculation that they could sign a deal with Google for one of those full gigawatt sites. Over the weekend, there were some rumors circulating on X that suggested that it would be a $33 billion deal over five years. That is highly problematic when you back into the implied dollars per megawatt (it is approximately $7 million per megawatt). The base is currently run-rating at $10 to $11 million. The Microsoft contract is worth about $11.5 million per megawatt.

So the question is, why would they do that? It is because they know they need to raise over $20 billion plus in debt over the next year that the market likely would rebuke, when you look at what is going on with hyperscaler CDS spreads and the Bitcoin miners. If they were to sign a deal like that, it would signal a lot of desperation. And the presenter does not think this is the type of stock that can work when numbers get cut, especially when there are terminal value concerns.

In terms of price target, the presenter believes that there is 25% downside from current levels based on DCF derived values from future contracted cash flows.
ideas.src: Michael Crespi <mcrespi@mchny.com> | MCH Idea Dinner Notes -- TMT -- August 10, 2026 | received 2026-08-12

ideas.th: Bumble is failing as Match outspends it 5x; once it exits, pricing and buybacks lift EPS growth to ~15% and the 11x P/E re-rates.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Match Group as a long.

Everybody knows what the company does. They have Hinge and Tinder. They compete with Bumble. The pitch comes down to the balance sheets and what is changing on the balance sheets. This company has an $8.5 billion market cap, and they have bought back $1 billion of stock in the last six quarters. Their competitor, Bumble, has a $700 million EV, and most of that is debt. And Bumble is really holding on for dear life right now—the stock is currently trading at $2.

The pitch comes down to the fact that the presenter thinks Bumble is going to be gone soon, and when and if that turns out to be true, Match will be a compelling long. It has not been a good long, as it has gone through a series of different CEOs. If you go back over the last 15 years, every three to four years it cycles to a new CEO. The presenter thinks the current CEO is good. He came from Zillow, Spencer Rascoff.

He is fixated on engagement, and you can start to see that in the metrics that are available through third parties. And the real visibility of that is, Bumble is failing. For reference, Match generates $3.5 billion in revenues while Bumble only generates $800 million in revenues, so four-to-one. And then Match outspends Bumble five to one in terms of marketing dollars. The presenter believe sit does not really matter who is on the app six months ago; what matters is who is coming onto the app tomorrow. And Match is outspending Bumble by 5x. You can see the engagement metrics, number of visits, minutes per visit—both of those are declining at Bumble. Whereas at Match and Tinder, they are growing, both those sets of metrics, and that is what the CEO of Match is fixated on.

Match’s growth is approximately 4% or 5%, but that is not the bet that you are making here. The bet is the P/E multiple, which is 12.5x this year and 11x next year, and that Bumble goes away and they start to modestly increase prices (across all their various tiers). For example, you hit this button for gold status, which enables you to download more photos. They have done a tremendous job on these initiatives in the past, which they are not talking about at the moment, because the presenter thinks their likely goal is to make sure Bumble is gone. Once Bumble is gone, then they can start to tweak things on the platform. And if there are only two apps you can download—one is more serious while the other is more casual—you have a lot of flexibility. That is the bet that the presenter is making.

If that happens, the buyback, which they are buying at a higher and higher price point—the presenter gave you the number earlier—they have bought 32 million shares at roughly $33 per share; the stock is at $37. But if you study the prices that they are buying at most recently, most recently in July, they bought it at $40, and the stock just dropped. So they have been active buyers at these levels, and they are retiring a decent amount of stock.

The bet is that pricing starts to lift from 4% to approximately 7% to 8%, and you get some margin accretion because they do not need to spend much on marketing. You should get an increase in the buyback, with EPS growth that looks more like +15%, and they are the only game in town. If that happens, then the presenter thinks the P/E multiple starts to shift, because the EPS right now, right here, it would look like 8x or 9x next year's EPS, in which case they think investors are likely willing to pay 14x to 15x for a company that is growing +8% to +9% with a decent visibility.

The presenter is not telling you it is a phenomenal industry. But what they have seen is, sometimes you get phenomenal stocks in industries that are not doing well, as competitors go away. Bumble is not going away tomorrow, but investors should keep it on their radar. The presenter thinks if they continue getting additional third-party data points that Bumble is about to fold, Match should work from the long side.

ideas.th: Silvus mesh-radio and D-Fend drone businesses growing 20-25% under conservative guidance; sees $25 2028 EPS vs Street $21.
ideas.cat: Anduril IPO; continued guidance raises on Silvus
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Motorola Solutions as a long.

Motorola Solutions has a $77 billion market cap, an $87 billion EV, and trades approximately $1 billion per day.

Motorola Solutions unifies communications, video, and security technology to protect people, property, and places across public safety and businesses. Approximately two-thirds of their business is used by first responders—such as ambulances, critical infrastructure, and communications within state and local municipalities.

The pitch is that in one-third of their business, revenues are growing approximately 20% to 25% due to recent acquisitions (this is separate from their stable LMR radio business, which is the critical infrastructure segment of their business that is growing low single digits with high margins and a sticky customer base with long-term contracts). The growth segment is in what is called mesh radio networks, which is used for drone technologies.

For example, one of the growth angles to the story that the presenter thinks will get picked up by investors when Anduril Industries eventually goes public, is that this software is essentially on (the presenter estimates) two-thirds of Anduril's devices.

In addition, them anagement team is very conservative. Every quarter they have been guiding up the acquisition of Silvus Technologies that closed approximately a year ago. They have what is called a “self-healing network”, meaning that if one of the local networks goes down, they can incorporate the other devices on the network and essentially be their own local network. That business is growing 25% per year, and every quarter they have guided those numbers higher.

The Street is assuming $21 per share of earnings in 2028. The presenter thinks they can generate $25 per share of earnings, between this deal and this other acquisition called D-Fend Solutions, which is a drone-capture technology, where they can essentially hack any drones that are in an area, and instead of shooting them down, they can essentially take them over and land them safely. That business is also growing mid-20%s at 50% EBITDA margins. That is where their variance comes from versus the Street and where their management is very conservative on these assumptions. They are currently supply constrained on all these products, but they are building facilities and have doubled their sales staff to meet this demand.

In summary, they have a customer base that is very sticky, with long-term contracts and high margins.

ideas.th: Contracted Google/Nvidia-backed leases worth $75-130/sh vs $86; Texas regulatory fear overdone and River Bend expansion coming.
ideas.cat: River Bend expansion; Texas regulatory clarity around November election
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Hut 8 as a long.

For background, the company has announced three contracts, which equate to $1.75 billion of NOI, with a third of it backed by Google and two-thirds backed by Nvidia. If you do a DCF of the lease payments, it is $75, and if you put a cap rate on it, it is $130. For reference, the stock is currently trading at $86.

In terms of the setup, the presenter believes there is a little bit of regulatory uncertainty based on the governor of Texas. And the presenter believes if Texas has problems with data centers, every other single pitch that is tied to data centers today would be trading lower than where they are currently trading.

In the presenter’s opinion, the Batch Zero processes that are funded by the biggest companies in the world, that have debt financing, that are going to be completed by great operators, are going to be approved. Two-thirds of the leases that the presenter mentioned, those that generate the $1.75 billion of NOI, come from the Batch Zero process, from the Corpus Christi asset of Hut 8. It is called the Beacon Point asset.

The presenter thinks that if this issue did not exist, the stock would be $20 or $30 higher. Investors have made a lot of money in it, so you have some investors taking profits. The presenter thinks this is an exceptional risk-reward, where you can deploy real capital and sleep at night knowing that you are going to make money. How much money obviously depends on how great the AI trade plays out from here.

But they have a River Bend facility where they are getting more power from Entergy, and the presenter believes Entergy wants to see some behind-the-meter investment by Hut 8, while Entergy invests to generate some of that power generation. Hut 8, the presenter believes, by the end of this year will announce an expansion of the River Bend project, which should be equal to what they have already announced in River Bend.

You should also get clarity in Texas—after the November election if not beforehand - via press releases, etc. In terms of the analyst community, one sell-side analyst’s price target, which does not give them full value for everything in the pipeline but gives enough value, is $250. The stock is currently trading at $86. The presenter thinks what has been announced, plus River Bend, plus behind the meter, should get them to a $150 price target.

And the presenter feels that the Situational Awareness unwind, the AI selloff, plus this Texas aspect, have put investors in a position where you can buy any Bitcoin miner and feel excited about the setup. You could buy Riot, and if they lease all of Corsicana it is probably worth $30-plus, but they have not really executed on much besides 25 megawatts to AMD. Core Scientific has done a lot of work with CoreWeave, but they have not announced too much, and their execution has been questioned by investors.

The presenter believes that the companies that have repeatedly delivered / executed for institutional investors are Hut 8 and Terawulf. Terawulf has announced contracts worth $17 to $19, and it is trading at $17 to $19 (the presenter believes it is still a good setup). Hut 8 has announced contracts likely worth $120, and they are likely going to announce additional positive updates, and they are viewed as good executors. The presenter feels like Hut 8 is likely the best risk-reward out of the group.

ideas.th: Bedrock monetizes multi-model inference tied to Anthropic/OpenAI ARR at higher margins, with room to raise compute pricing; 22x $18 2028 EPS.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Amazon.com as a long.

The presenter acknowledges that this is not a controversial call, but the way they are thinking about it currently is, there is still a lot of upside even after this move. The presenter knows it is not up a lot on a year to date basis, but it is up a lot post-CY 2Q earnings. The presenter believes it is worth $400 in the near term (EPS of $18 in 2028 using a 22x multiple, which equates to a $400 target price).

The piece to the story that the presenter is excited about is the piece that they think investors are starting to come around to, which is Bedrock. It is a smaller part of the AWS AI platform. The presenter has always thought frontier model—frontier, frontier, frontier - open source does not matter. The presenter thinks in the last six months to nine months, it has become clearer that, whether it is going to be open source or not, companies are more committed to being multi-model, meaning they want to be able to use Anthropic or OpenAI, or they might also want to bring in Kimi or some of the other open-source models.

So the presenter has been trying to figure out ways to express that view. They think there are a few business models in the private markets to express this view like Baseten, Fireworks, and some of the other inference clouds. In the presenter's view, the best way, at least at their scale, to express the view that companies are going multi-model is through the cloud providers. Particularly, each one of them has a version of this - Bedrock, Foundry, and Vertex—that is for Amazon, Microsoft, and Google respectively. For reference, Bedrock's is much larger.

At the end of the day, you have a line in the Amazon business model and in the Microsoft-Google business model that is tied directly to Anthropic and OpenAI's ARR growth, because some percentage of the tokens accessed for Anthropic and OpenAI are being accessed through Bedrock, Foundry, and Vertex. That has started showing up in terms of revenue growth—it is the CAPEX converting to revenue growth—but also it is showing up in terms of higher EBIT margins, because these token-as-a-service products that are offered through Bedrock come at a marginally higher EBIT margin, which is also good for the business. The presenter does not have a view on Nebius or CoreWeave—but this is their differentiated worldview on Amazon that gets them excited. If you do the rough math on the numbers that are out there—for Anthropic as an example, and this is likely a conservative number that investors are talking about—but if they end the year at $100 billion of ARR and they have two or three gigawatts of compute, that means they are monetizing that compute at $50 billion per gigawatt (you can do it on megawatts, but let us just say $50 billion per gigawatt). The cloud providers are currently charging between ~$10 to $12 billion per gigawatt to rent that compute space, so the presenter estimates the labs are doing 80% to 90% inference margins.

It probably does not stay that high, but to the presenter, that is an exciting thing happening in the market. The end consumers of labs are growing what they are able to monetize at faster than the clouds are scaling their price. The presenter does not know how to conceptualize it, but there is certainly room for the clouds to raise their price, particularly when Anthropic and OpenAI are scooping up every bit of compute. And then there is a spillover into the marginal suppliers of compute, like the Nebiuses and CoreWeaves. The presenter has not thought enough about that yet.

But to the presenter, if your main customer is earning somewhere upwards of 80% margins, there is probably room for that cost to go up. That is another pricing lever on the cloud businesses that gets the presenter excited in terms of their longer-term view. They do think investors have come around to the fact that the CAPEX they are spending is producing faster revenue growth, but there are other levers that are exciting.

The company specializes in designing high-speed connectivity solutions for data centers and AI infrastructure. The whole idea is that if you continue to connect clusters, you need more scale-up switch. And surprisingly, there is no merchant in scale up switch. Right now you have some competitors in the space like Broadcom, but the presenter thinks that a lot of these customers buying other XPUs do not want to be beholden to Broadcom, where traditionally they were not a great supplier to many of these customers.

ideas.th: Jeol holds >50% share in spot e-beam tools needed for indium phosphide lasers, not in Street numbers; mid-teens P/E vs Aixtron 30x.
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Jeol Ltd. as a long.

The presenter likens Jeol to the ASML of optical. The presenter would also argue that it is cheap on an absolute and relative basis, and that the company is not well followed by investors.

The presenter believes it is a high-quality company. Their long-term operating margins are somewhat in the 40% range for their industrial segment, which is the segment the presenter cares about. They also have a really deep R&D moat, so they are not an over-earning commodity type business or anything like that.

For reference, the ticker is 6951 JP. It is a Japanese company. They have roughly a $2.5 billion market cap. Just for context, in terms of the stock and the fundamentals, they have been roughly steady—not explosive growth or anything like that—in the past few years. This is in part because their core businesses are more so tied to tools that make EUV masks. They are more levered to SKU count as opposed to volumes. It could be analogous to EDA, so that is why the business has been somewhat steady.

But the hidden gem and the crux of the thesis is that they have a front-end tool that every optical company—like Lumentum, Coherent, & Dongshan—needs to create indium phosphide and also CW (ultra-high-power lasers). From all their checks, it is clear that companies are increasing CAPEX and trying to expand capacity (the presenter believes approximately greater than 5x for this indium phosphide over the next five years). The question is, how do you play this theme through picks and shovels? This is one way you can do it. The market, it seems like they have already discovered the Lam of optical, which the presenter would argue is Aixtron in Germany, which trades at a hefty multiple (30x calendar 2027 EPS). But the market is missing the opportunity to invest in JEOL, which the presenter believes is the ASML of optical, and only trades at a mid-teens multiple on calendar 2027 EPS. The presenter believes that practically no optical revenue is baked into Street assumptions / numbers.

So the part that the presenter really cares about for JEOL is the spot e-beam tool. What that does is, it uses super precise electron beams to physically carve the gradients on the indium phosphide lasers. For reference, tool demand scales with how many lasers you want to create. This is exactly what benefits companies like Coherent and others.

The presenter would note, in this market for spot e-beam tools, this company has greater than 50% share. And then from the presenter's bottoms-up work with indium phosphide, it seems like the market will need greater than 300 tools over the next few years (call it $3 million per for these tools). So all in, this might add 10% to 20% top-line growth on top of what the Street has assumed, simply from this segment alone, which is the segment that the presenter cares about.

Again, the Street is assuming very minimal growth for this company overall, call it low-single-digit, mid-single-digit percent growth. The presenter thinks it could be 10% to 15% above that, just from the spot e-beam. Based on a fair multiple—25x calendar 2027—and using the presenter's numbers, the stock should be a double from here. The hidden gem is the spot e-beam. They literally help you create more indium phosphide. They are a toolmaker that can participate in that.

ideas.th: All-stock ON Semi acquisition target; ON fell 25% on deal wiping out premium, so SYNA is a proxy long ON as earnings reset narrative (26x vs peers 30x)
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Synaptics as a long.

They were recently acquired by ON Semiconductor. The deal is an all-stock deal with a 20% premium. The day after the deal was announced, ON Semiconductor’s stock traded down 25%, effectively wiping out the premium.

The presenter observed in the last couple of months, these stock-swap deals have been absolutely pummeled, based on the fact that any acquisition that drifts from the current narrative creates selling pressure. However, this creates a pretty interesting dynamic / setup.

The deal itself and the rationale behind the deal is very forward-looking. It does dilute a bit of ON Semi’s expertise and the narrative of them in data centers-or just capitalizing on being prominent in data centers-but also camera sensors and EVs. So, it is a little story-dilut ive, but on the financial front, it is pretty much a wash. They bought it at a decent multiple and paid a pretty low premium.

The presenter’s pitch is Synaptics long, by proxy to have exposure to ON Semi. Because the deal dynamics of this deal are going to be far into next year. They are going to have a long regulatory process, but that does not necessarily matter. Looking at the comps, ON Semi is down 25%. The entire comp set took a leg down but recovered and is only down 5%. The clearing catalyst for this — and what it has been for some of these merger-related sell-offs — is earnings. As long as earnings hold up, it will help reset the narrative.

Over the last nine months, the stock had traded in line with peers at 30x P/E. It is now trading at 26x P/E. The presenter sees 15% upside in the very near term. Fortunately, the presenter believes TXNM and NXPI are going to be helpful earnings prints beforehand, to see if anything has materially shifted. But being long Synaptics itself, with the deal dynamics, since it is all stock, you will capture almost all of the upside in ON Semi.

But when it comes to the downside, Synaptics’ peers themselves have been performing well.

The standalone value of Synaptics is where it is currently trading. And if ON Semi were to trade down, the presenter gets additional optionality when it comes to potential interlopers, but also the deal dynamics potentially being voted down.

It is a $30 stock, with a $10 billion market cap, $9 billion of debt, generating $2.7 billion of EBITDA, and $700 million of free cash flow going to $1.5 billion. The presenter thinks the core business is bottoming. Subscribers could turn positive in the back half. They have spent almost $1 billion of CAPEX over the last three years, re-platforming to get more uplink/downlink data on their customers. That will likely lead to an ARPU uplift starting in the back half as well.

The presenter thinks the core to the thesis is their spectrum. If you look at the EchoStar / SpaceX deal, then more recently, Iridium getting bought by Rocket Lab, that was only 10 megahertz. And when you think through the recent regulatory changes at the FCC around this — it is called “Space Abundance for Weird Space Stuff,” which is basically SpaceX asking for certain changes in how spectrum is allocated, how it is used, and the ability to lease it. For context, Sirius owns 35 megahertz of prime lower S-band spectrum. It is worth noting, the presenter has been a spectrum bear for 10 years, but they think there are legitimate use cases now for the first time. You are seeing that play out, with EchoStar and Rocket Lab.

The current Sirius XM management team is already migrating their core users from the lower 12-and-a-half to the upper 12-and-a-half, which is going to unlock some value. But in the meantime, this new regulatory change at the FCC is going to allow them to lease the uplink part of certain pieces of their megahertz. And why does that matter? The uplink part will allow, if anyone puts a satellite in space that is running a data center, they have specific spectrum that is very good at operating that specific satellite.

Tesla has been pretty overt about wanting more data on anything related to the car, and Elon has been pretty overt on SpaceX for wanting more capacity for various use cases within SpaceX. The presenter does not think it is a huge leap to say that a Tesla would want to own the spectrum within Sirius XM. This is not necessarily a consensus view, but when you put it all together and look at all the regulatory changes that have come out, it seems like it would be a natural fit. If you use some of these recent transactions as comps, you get anywhere from 50% to 100% upside versus the current stock price.

ideas.th: Ned Fleming's (Construction Partners) Sun Belt ready-mix roll-up buying at 4-6x vs 13x multiple with margin uplift; 30% EBITDA CAGR 2026-30
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Suncrete as a long.

Suncrete has a $1.4 billion market cap, and trades approximately $9.5 million per day.

Suncrete recently de-SPACed in April. The presenter thinks it is an extremely under-followed, extremely attractive roll-up story in the ready-mix concrete industry, and they think ultimately this will be a long-term compounder. It is led by Ned Fleming, this being his follow-up venture after Construction Partners (ROAD). That was a similar roll-up strategy in the asphalt industry, and that ended up being a 10-bagger since its 2018 IPO.

In terms of ready-mix concrete, it is a logistics business. It is inherently very local, and that makes it extremely fragmented. Specifically in the Sun Belt region, which is where Suncrete is targeting, there are approximately 700 operators, and 90% of those operators own less than five plants. So, it is extremely fragmented.

In terms of the roll-up algorithm Suncrete is trying to achieve, they are acquiring these businesses at ~4x to 6x EBITDA. The stock currently trades at 13x, so you automatically capture that. Also, there is a large margin uplift story here as well. These targets have approximately mid-teens EBITDA margins. The company has approximately 20% EBITDA margins, and they think they can get these targets there through purchasing power, asset utilization, and back-office consolidation.

In terms of financing for the acquisitions, they raised about $225 million through the SPAC.

Last week, they also increased their leverage capacity. In the presenter’s opinion, they will go up to 3x on deals near term, but this is a very free-cash-flow-generative business. There is high conversion (approximately 60%), there is low maintenance CAPEX, and ultimately, they will organically get down to their target of 2x to 2.5x.

In terms of competition for acquisitions, there is not much. The aggregates companies are deemphasizing ready-mix. They are getting out of this business after a lot of failed experimentation. There is a large private roll-up called SRM; they are constrained by very high leverage (approximately 6x levered). So, there are plenty of opportunities for Suncrete to take advantage of, where they can become the acquirer of choice, since they maintain the family name on the door and they do not cut staff right away (they are not like a typical private equity business).

In terms of organic growth, their management is underwriting 8% to 10% organic growth, which is made up half by price and half by volume. In the presenter’s view, this seems credible, given the region they are targeting (the Sun Belt), which has very strong demographic trends – such as reshoring, infrastructure rebuild, and data centers. Data centers, it is worth noting, have hundreds of thousands of cubic yards of concrete. So, these are huge projects. And a lot of these mom-and-pop competitors that could be next door to a huge data center development, do not have the capacity or the desire to actually pursue these kinds of growth projects, which Suncrete will happily step into.

In terms of the overall growth algorithm, the presenter thinks they can do a 30% EBITDA CAGR from 2026 to 2030. This is underwritten by 6% organic growth, an average of $30 million acquired EBITDA per year, and then margin uplift. It is also worth noting that Ned, his private equity firm, and management / the board own approximately 46% of the company.

In terms of catalysts from here, the presenter expects to see more acquisitions. The presenter believes they will get to $130 million of EBITDA exiting 2026, and they will be able to scale up acquisitions even more than that. In terms of a target price, they presenter believes it is worth $28 per share, or 40% upside versus where it is currently trading.

ideas.th: Down from $400+ on Berkshire unwind, destocking and competition; at bottom of new-build and maintenance cycles as new CEO's SG&A cuts restore leverage
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Pool Corp. as a long.

For context, Leslie’s, which is one of their main suppliers recently saw its stock plunge nearly 50%. Essentially, they stocked too much inventory into a hostile channel. This has been a well-documented phenomenon over the last couple of years. Leslie’s is losing market share, and their inability to serve, combined with massively exploding margins, has made them the persona non grata in the industry. However, the presenter does not necessarily think that reflects poorly on Pool Corp.

Back to what has been pressuring the stock year to date; it is back down to $200 per share, a full $96 lower than when Berkshire got involved. Obviously, in the presenter’s opinion, the power struggle at Berkshire led to a massive seller given the unwind of the portfolio. They got de-indexed, which was extremely predictable. Additionally, they had to deal with the massive destocking in the pool industry as well as fluctuations in interest rates, plus increased competition from Heritage moving into the space. All of this has led to the stock going from $400 + at its peak to $200 currently.

What the presenter thinks happens over the course of the next six months is that you are going to get a new CEO and new management team. They are going to hit numbers. The presenter thinks once th at momentum gets going with a string of decent quarters, you can start to see massive value capture, because this is a company with a very strong moat.

So, you have a good business that is at trough, that is going to hopefully benefit from improving economics on the new construction / residential side. If you run the math on how the repair-remodel cycle has been going, the installed base that will need service over the course of the next couple of years, as a percentage of what is being serviced right now, it is running at the lowest maintenance utilization ever.

So, the presenter believes you are catching the bottom of two cycles. You do not need the residential or new construction to come back in earnest. You simply need them to hit numbers and for the high-end consumer not to fall off the cliff. That is not necessarily a call on what is going to happen there. But the presenter thinks that this is an interesting opportunity with a lot of negative catalysts, and now they are on the other side of it, and the presenter thinks a new CEO would also benefit the story.

Also worth noting, the company is highly focused on SG&A management, and the way that they are going about it is quite surgical. It reminds the presenter of where MSC Industrial was at the beginning of the year. The new CEO actually has their priorities in order, understands all the problems with the compensation of their associates, how to handle seasonal employees, and how to address the issues that are endemic in the business and why they are not getting operating leverage the way that they should. That is an incredibly powerful tool for improving a business model that essentially just operates on channel density and managing seasonal SG&A trends on a quarter-over-quarter basis. You have some one that actually wants to take costs out of the business and is not just living off of the legacy of being one of the best-run companies from the 2000 to 2019 period.

The math is, if there are not significant downward revisions to EBITDA next year, even if they are 8% below and it gets back to historical relative trading multiples, it is worth $350.

Take a discount to that — a pretty significant discount to it, just to account for building products peers broadly, or building products distributors broadly derating-it is worth $305.

It is currently trading at $210. So, the upside is not the issue. The presenter thinks the issue is that there needs to be credibility around the story and they need a new CEO.

ideas.th: At 75% of book with stable $1B potash EBITDA while Hormuz sulfur shock idles phosphate; depleted soil bank and China export ban set up sharp phosphate recovery
ideas.cat: Strait of Hormuz reopening; spring planting
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Mosaic as a long.

In terms of the setup, the presenter acknowledges that this is more of a wait-and-see story.

But you have a "mission critical for farmers" type supplier trading at 75% of book value, in one of the worst situations that you could ever be in as a fertilizer supplier (all hinging on the Straight of Hormuz).

Primarily, their business is split in two. They make phosphate fertilizers for US farmers. They have 75% market share in the US. The other part of the business is an incredibly stable potash business, which generates $1 billion of EBITDA per year. Supply/demand in Potash is in balance, and prices are stable to up slightly higher. They are the low-cost supplier. That is the segment keeping them afloat.

The phosphate business is the segment that is currently a mess. The biggest input to phosphate is sulfur (you need approximately 0.5 tons of sulfur to produce 1 ton of phosphate so it is clearly a large input cost). Approximately 50% of the sulfur supply is locked up in the Strait of Hormuz. Sulfur prices have gone from approximately $200 per ton to approximately $850 + per ton. And while phosphate fertilizer prices have closely followed sulfur higher, they have gotten so elevated that US farmers can no longer afford to buy them. So they are simply not buying and demand has been decimated.

Mosaic has been forced to shut down ~30% of capacity. There are three main suppliers in the world; all of them have shut anywhere from 30% to 50% of supply. Now the breakpoint here is that farmers can only hold off using phosphate fertilizer for so long, otherwise you risk yield compression and a potential global food shortage. Unlike urea or nitrogen, you can skip seasons of phosphate application. In terms of phosphate fertilizer, you can think about it as a soil bank. You can top up to 100%. If you do not refill one season, you are down to 70%.

If you do not refill again, you are down to 30%. We are now down to 30%, and if they skip again, they theoretically risk having horrible yields and a food shortage. That, the presenter presumes, would occur by the spring of next year.

In the presenter’s opinion, the Trump administration has no idea what to do here. The market is broken. Corn is not expensive enough for farmers to have enough money to buy fertilizer. So, you are sitting here with a company that has just shut production and will sit on the free cash flow from the potash segment of the business and wait for the market to eventually recover. But when the market recovers, it gets really good. So on half of their business, the presenter expects zero EBITDA. In total, consensus estimates have them generating $1.4 billion of EBITDA. Should the phosphate fertilizer market recover, and Mosaic can generate anywhere close to historical margins, EBITDA in 2027 could be anywhere from $2.6 billion to $3 billion of EBITDA. So, you are looking at a stock that is currently trading at $22 per share versus a book value of $30 per share. The presenter’s base case is $30 to $45, but there is a real chance that the stock could trade as high as $60 to $70 next year if the Strait of Hormuz opens and sulfur flows again.

The last thing the presenter would mention is, China was dumping phosphate fertilizer into this market to the tune of 10% to 15% of volume essentially flooding the market. China now needs that sulfur — one, for their own domestic fertilizer, but two, because lithium phosphate batteries are growing so fast that it is an industry they are going to cater to. They have banned all exports of sulfur and phosphate from the country starting this year, and the presenter does not think that gets pulled. On top of the 30% of the major producers, you are taking out another 10% of raw material from China.

ideas.th: Largest independent SSP with CTV growing 30%; Google ad tech behavioral remedies could add 400-500bp share, lifting EPS from $1.20 to $2+
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Magnite as a long.

This is an ad tech company with a $2.9 billion market cap. The stock currently trades a t $20 per share with a $70 million ADV.

For most investors, when you hear “ad tech”, the first thing that likely comes to mind is The Trade Desk. The Trade Desk is on the demand side and has some headwinds from new competition and some other competitive factors. Magnite sits on the other side of the equation (on the supply side). They have close partnerships with the publishers of the big streaming platforms, from Netflix to Warner Bros Discovery and Disney, and then also increasingly with commerce media platforms like an Expedia or a Walmart, or companies of that sort which have proprietary data on their customers. And while The Trade Desk might handle the bidding, this company sits very close to the actual spot where the ad sits and is able to essentially run the auction.

The core story is that they have a legacy business, tied to desktop and mobile, that is stabilizing. But now, more than half of revenue ex-TAC comes from connected TV, and that grew 30% in the most recent quarter. So, the ex-TAC revenue on a consolidated basis grew over 10%. It is a pretty good trajectory, growth is accelerating, and the core backdrop positions the company to be able to generate $1.20 of earnings in 2027. It trades at 16x-16.5x next year’s estimate. That is the core story. It is well positioned, it has ramping partnerships, and general CTV growth is the driver for the business.

But the special situation angle to the story is tied to Google. Approximately a year ago, in April 2025, Google was ruled to have violated anti-trust law by monopolizing the publisher ad server and ad exchange (SSP) markets, creating structural advantages for its own exchange versus independent SSPs like Magnite. So now the focus shifts to what remedies the court will ultimately impose.

A year ago, there was volatility in the stock, because there was an initial assumption that Google would be forced to do a structural remedy and potentially break up. And then, when investors realized that would likely not happen, the stock traded down. But in the presenter’s opinion, that misses the opportunity here. What is likely going to happen is some form of behavioral remedies, which would level the playing field between Google’s ad exchange and independent SSPs, allowing Magnite to compete more fairly for publisher inventory.

Magnite is the largest independent supply-side platform, with approximately 6% total share where Google controls ~60%. If you apply a similar market share that they have within the 40% outside of Google, you get 9 points of potential share gain. Every 100 basis points of SSP share gain is worth roughly $50 million of incremental contribution ex-TAC with approximately ~90% flow through to EBITDA. If they are able to capture 400 or 500 basis points of share gain with those behavioral remedies, rather than $1.20 of earnings, earnings power could be greater than $2 of earnings. Applying a 16.5x multiple on that equates to a $33 stock price or 65% upside from current levels.

On the behavioral side, the positive is that the appeal process could be shorter and the implementation phase could be as quick as a year. If there was a structural outcome, that could ultimately create greater long-term upside, but it would likely be held up in a much longer appeal and implementation process. As a result, behavioral remedies could allow the earnings upside to be realized much sooner. And again, the earnings opportunity is very attractive.

ideas.th: Two project-financed AI shells leased 15 yrs to Google and Nvidia yield ~$7.50/sh NOI (worth ~$150) vs $87 ex-cash; expansions could lift NOI to ~$20
ideas.cat: Nvidia ROFR expansion (this month); Louisiana PSC expansion approval
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Hut 8 as a Long.

Hut 8 has a $12 billion market cap with no holding company debt. They own two shells that they are close to having fully built out; one in Texas called Deacon Point, and one in Louisiana called River Bend. Each are leased. Leases commence in the second half of next year and in early 2028. The leases, one is to Google; the other is to, if you read the debt documents behind the lease, Nvidia. Each of the two projects are project-financed, with investment-grade ratings attached to them. Against the investment-grade rating, they are being 100% debt-financed. There is no net equity being put up at the holding company against either lease.

When the two leases are built out and start to generate income, the presenter believes that the company will be generating $7.50 per share of NOI combined from the two leases. One is 450 megawatts; the other is approximately 360 megawatts. Each of those two leases has expansion options against that $7.50 of NOI. With $10 in cash and effectively Bitcoin at the holding company, you are paying $97 per share today. The presenter thinks the $7.50 is worth $150.

Investors have raised questions about the duration and repeatability of the lease at expiration. Each lease is a 15-year lease with CPI escalators, with 15-year extension options (at the option of the lessee). The debt markets have funded the capital against those two projects at 6.2% and 6.3%. A lender to the project cares a lot about its ability to get the lease, because they want to get the maturity back when it expires. The debt matches the lease term of the project.

The company has signed leases which offer a higher price per megawatt hour than any lease that has been signed by any development company of a shell or former Bitcoin miner previously, until the Wu lf lease that got announced last week (which is a bit higher). Pricing generally has trended higher. Execution risk in building the shells — through the presenter’s very extensive diligence, including talking to all the subs and sending people to the sites — seems to be very low.

What is exciting about Hut 8 is not that you are investing in it at a 7.5% cap and it should trade to a 5%. What is exciting is each of the two leases has extension options. The Texas lease to Nvidia, Nvidia has the right of first refusal on capacity to double the size of that project, plus or minus. That right of first refusal expires this month. If it is not exercised, the presenter thinks there will be demand for that asset again. The power is there. It is on the grid; it was being used for something else. There is no regulatory risk. The presenter thinks that there is a very large bid for compute, and you have a lot of optionality there. On the Google asset, they have the ability to more than double the capacity they are leasing to Google, pending regulatory approval in Louisiana. The presenter thinks the Louisiana PSC is receiving legislative and government pressure to approve the expansion. It is adding capacity to the grid, but there are a lot of tax dollars and job creation (temporarily at least) too. The presenter also thinks the politics in that jurisdiction are very favorable for development, at a time when politics for development are increasingly tenuous. These stocks are down a lot on the Meta release, on the unwind in momentum stocks, and on today’s New York State one-year moratorium. The presenter does not think any of those issues extend to this company in any way, shape, or form.

In addition, they have more than 2,000 gigawatts of power that they are trying to develop and lease out as shells to hyperscalers. In the presenter’s view, the optionality around that is all upside. If you assume both leases get extended, that $7.50 per share of NOI, at the same price per megawatt hour, will be closer to $20 of NOI for a stock that is currently trading at $97 per share less $10 of cash and Bitcoin, so it is closer to $87. The setup seems asymmetric to the presenter.

The presenter thinks a lot of AI is about whether or not you want to play, but also, if you do, where you want to play. There are lots of different ways to play. A way that has very little downside — arguably none — and a huge amount of potential upside seems to be a good way to play in the presenter’s view.

ideas.th: American Axle/Dowlais merger at <4x EBITDA; $300M synergies, metal forming margin recovery, powder metallurgy spin and deleveraging can double the stock
ideas.pt: ~2x in two years; low-mid teens bull
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Dauch Corp. as a long.

Dauch trades at under 4x EBITDA. It is the merger between Dowlais and American Axle. It trades $25 million per day. It has $4.2 billion in net debt, a $1.2 billion market cap, and the stock is currently trading at $5.25.

They operate two segments. The driveline segment, which combines American Axle’s legacy driveline business and Dowlais’ automotive business (that segment makes axle s, side shafts, and other transmission parts). Then the metal forming segment, which is comprised of the American Axle metal forming business, which makes various steel parts that go into the axles. And then the powder metallurgy segment, which is comprised of smaller precision parts. It is a bit of a different process and not very synergistic. In the presenter’s opinion, they have implied they could potentially spin that segment off (but the presenter notes that nothing is official). That business generates close to $200 million of EBITDA, and if they sold it for 5.5x EBITDA, and the RemainCo. stayed at a similar multiple — possibly re-rated to 4x — that would add close to $2 per share and would take net debt below the 2.5x leverage target.

As it relates to the synergy targets, they have laid out a path to $300 million from this Dowlais merger that occurred in February (on a COGS base of $9 billion, and SG&A is $1.3 billion combined). The presenter believes that they will be able to better in-source the forgings and gain purchasing power on the steel and metal, as well as some overlapping operations facilities.

At the segment level, American Axle’s legacy metal forming business used to be a high-teens margin business. After facing some labor issues during COVID and a lot of mismanagement of inventory, the margins troughed at 6% in 2023. Now they have gotten back to almost 8%, and if those can get back to just 10%, that would drive an additional $50 million of EBITDA.

And finally, in terms of North American auto production, you do not need to underwrite any sort of inflection; it simply needs to remain here at mid-cycle levels (15 million is the guide for this year).

On valuation, the presenter thinks you can get to a double in two years simply from achieving half of the synergies, the multiple holding, and the company deleveraging to 2.2x.

If you believe that there is some pickup in auto production, a potential spin-off of the powder metallurgy business, or margin improvement on the metal forming segment, you could get to a low-to-mid-teens stock price.

ideas.th: Top litigation/antitrust economics consultancy riding M&A rebound; forgivable-loan accounting masks ~$140M true EBITDA vs ~$90M screens, 14% adj FCF yield
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Charles River as a long.

Charles River has a $1 billion market cap and trades approximately $25 million per day.

There is no fixed debt (seasonal revolver) on the business whatsoever. It is down about 20% in the last six months on general AI disintermediation fears.

They are the number one legal consultant. They have done work with 98 of the 100 top law firms in the last two years, and they are known for doing your complex M&A work. For example, if you are doing the $80 billion Hewlett-Packard merger, they are doing the expert witness testimonies, Hart-Scott-Rodino (HSR) review, and defining what the market is, which has become more important. Defining and supporting these difficult questions relating to an industry such as, what is a handbag market? Or, what is a gate market for airports? Any kind of regulatory challenge, including state challenges (Paramount for example), is another tailwind for the business. So, they are highly levered to M&A activity picking up, which is up approximately 30% year over year.

The event-driven catalyst here is that the presenter believes Q1 expectations are very conservative. If you look at the last ten years, they have always raised full-year guidance in Q2, because the first half of the year pretty much mirrors the second half of the year, so in the presenter’s opinion, that is when they get the confidence to do it.

But the stock screens poorly at the moment. If you look at CapIQ, they are generating ~$90 million of EBITDA on a trailing 12-month basis. If you make an adjustment for what the presenter is about to mention, they think it is closer to $140 million. They have mentioned it is record EBITDA margins. The cash from ops gets reduced by ~$89 million in the LTM period because they use what they call forgivable loans. To bring these expert witnesses in house, these PhDs, these small teams, they do a forgivable loan. It might be a $5 million cash outlay day zero (with claw back protections for CRAI), and you amortize $1 million per year for five years. They cannot add back any of that amortization, and they get hit for the full 100% cash outflow in their cash flow statement. And they have been staffing up. They see a lot of demand. Their utilization is at record highs currently.

In terms of the setup, the presenter believes you have this GAAP-to-cash convergence story, where the presenter thinks they are going to easily generate $140 million in EBITDA in the next 12 months. There are only two sell-side analysts covering the company who assume EBITDA is closer to $90 million, which is very off base in the presenter’s view. It is 9.2x EV to EBITDA and a 14% free cash flow yield if you make these adjustments. They have not confirmed when earnings are yet, but the presenter thinks August 6th to August 9th, where they are likely going to revise full-year guidance higher. You are going to see these adjustments over the next couple of quarters roll off. They are going to show record operating margins, and they should continue to ride the M&A wave moving forward.

ideas.th: Anywhere deal doubles share; luxury K-shaped housing exposure and lifting Anywhere agent productivity drive EBITDA ~30% above Street
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Compass as a long.

Compass currently has a $9 billion market cap and a $12 billion EV.

They are the largest real estate brokerage in the US, with 20% market share in terms of transaction value, and 12% market share in terms of transactions. The presenter thinks it is an industry that is going to continue to consolidate and become better over time. The presenter thinks Compass has scale benefits, brand benefits, technology benefits, and network effect benefits. The presenter sees the industry on the residential side evolving similar to the commercial side over time. The presenter thinks Compass becomes similar to a CBRE on the residential side. That is the sort of paradigm that they use.

In terms of the thesis, there are some themes that the presenter likes, and then some idiosyncratic factors they like. On the industry thematic side, the presenter does not know when the housing market will turn. But what is interesting is, existing home sales are pretty close to the bottom or bouncing along the bottom. And the way the presenter gets there is, if you look at quantifying the structural floor for existing home sales (reason for move being either death, divorce, and relocation/growing family) these "recurring" activities get you close to today's home sales levels. The presenter does not think it gets much worse from here.

And then, maybe more importantly, the presenter thinks Compass is a beneficiary of the “K-shaped recovery.” The average home where they help facilitate the transaction is close to $1 million dollars in value. When you look underneath the hood, while the housing market is very depressed, the luxury market is actually doing very well. Luxury volumes are growing approximately mid-single digit and average price is growing mid-single digit. The presenter thinks, from a macro standpoint, they are — to use a bad pun — in the right neighborhood.

And then on the idiosyncratic side, they closed the transaction of Anywhere (the old Realogy). The deal doubled their market share. There is a lot of OPEX takeout opportunity that the presenter does not think they have a particularly differentiated view on. Where the presenter is differentiated is on the revenue side. Basically, what Compass did when they started was, they recruited the best agents and gave them advantageous splits. The presenter thinks Compass has essentially cornered the market for the most talented, productive agents.

On average, their agents do ten deals a year. The average agent at Anywhere does five. The presenter does not think five goes to ten, but they think five goes to more than five. The presenter thinks there is a lot of potential revenue upside that they are not communicating.

They are sort of marketing things like back-office, tech, and SG&A. The presenter thinks a big part of the vision of the deal is getting the Anywhere agents to be a lot more productive. The presenter thinks very highly of the management team. And there is other optionality on the MLS side which the presenter is happy to discuss further.

The presenter is ~30% above the Street in terms of EBITDA (that is primarily revenue-based).

The presenter runs three scenarios. One is a tepid housing market with the presenter’s revenue upside; that gets them to like $17 per share from $12 currently. They assume a 10x multiple, which on a synergized basis, it is trading closer to 9x right now, but the presenter thinks business quality is going up. In a scenario where the housing market sees some level of recovery, the presenter believes it is a low - $20s stock (predicated primarily on volume).

And if the presenter is dead wrong and they do not get the revenue synergy, they just get the cost synergy, and the housing market stays flat, they think it is a $8 or $9 stock. So, the presenter thinks the skew is attractive.

ideas.th: Rushed cable/NBCU spin echoes WBD; high tax-basis media assets could enable a taxable spin and sale (e.g., NBCU+Sky to Netflix) before administration ends
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Comcast as a long.

The presenter believes that Comcast has echoes of potentially a WBD. They have announced a spin-off. Yes, the CEO seemed pretty adamant. He said the spin-off is absolutely not being done for M&A. That was on the spin-off call. But if you go back to the spin-off call, that took most investors by surprise. It was only a 25-minute call. There was no active Q&A — it was all pre-submitted questions — and it has very much the air of a rushed decision.

The breakup will be, on the one hand, the cable business. Investors think Charter is a natural partner there. The SpinCo would be the media NBCU business, which is studios plus parks, plus NBC Sports, and then Sky. That is a little bit more of a complicated asset.

What the presenter would submit is that the media side is actually pretty interesting. If you think about WBD, remember that initially they were going to sell just one piece to Netflix.

And the way they were going to do that is, they actually flipped around the spin, so they would do a taxable spin of the networks. And the question that the presenter has, is a taxable spin possible here?

The presenter does not think it would be at the cable business, because cable is probably heavily depreciated and the tax base is low. But if you think about how that media co was built — it was the acquisition of NBCU, it was the acquisition of Sky — and those assets likely have pretty discoverable and relatively high tax bases. With that being said, the presenter thinks it is an interesting stock at an interesting time. You have the Charter-Cox, Liberty Broadband deal likely closing in August. You have the administration that has two years left. Is all this being done to potentially prepare for one last transaction? Does Netflix care for NBCU plus Sky?

ideas.th: Montana SAF online earning ~$4/gal vs Street ~$1 on 150M gallons; Phase 2 cheaper (<$300M) than feared and Shell offtake partner a likely acquirer
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Calumet as a long.

In terms of the setup, there are a bunch of catalysts that have been realized, but the market has not quite priced them correctly.

For background, Calumet has a traditional refinery in Shreveport Louisiana, that produces 77,000 barrels per day. Of that, 22,000 barrels are used for what is called performance brands (i.e. high-end motor oils and things like that). That part of the business generates ~$60 million of EBITDA at very high margin. They sold a piece of that business last year at 10x EBITDA, so the presenter thinks putting a 10x multiple on $60 million is the right number.

They also have a more crack-spread-oriented business in that refinery. It is approximately 55,000 barrels. That business is performing very well currently with crack spreads where they are, generating approximately $300 million of EBITDA.

But the real story is the ir Montana Renewables asset. It was a renewable diesel refinery in Montana, which was strategically located for both the inputs and for their end markets. That just went online producing sustainable aviation fuel, for which they have off-take agreements on approximately 70% to 80% of the first 150 million barrels of production (which began in May). They are at spot on the balance, right when prices are on fire. The off-take agreements are at approximately $1.50 above renewable diesel. Renewable diesel margins currently are ~$3, so they are earning ~$4 after costs on 150 million gallons. The presenter underwrote $2.50 initially, so this is materially above where they think it is going to be. The Street is modeling only $1 of earnings on that, so they are very far off.

Also worth noting, the second phase of the SAF expansion, which the presenter thinks they will talk about on the Q2 earnings call, is one of the catalysts. Investors are not modeling that. In the presenter’s opinion, investors think it is going to cost $600 or $700 million to build out phase two for the next 150 million gallons. The presenter thinks it is going to be under $300 million. In the meantime, this company is going to be cash flowing $500 or $600 million per year at the current rates. The off-take agreements they have, one of them is with Shell. Ultimately, the presenter thinks Shell buys the whole company in the next 12 months.

But investors realizing how much production they are getting out of their initial SAF production is going to be a positive catalyst. The margins they are capturing is going to be a positive catalyst. The lack of cost of developing the second half of the 150 million gallons is going to be a third catalyst. And then, like the presenter said, they think Shell ultimately buys the whole company.

ideas.th: Accounting scandal quantified (EBIT overstated 5-10%); data center/power (40% of EBIT) drives teens-20% EPS growth to ¥240 by FY3/29; good/bad co split optional
ideas.cat: Financial update by end Sept; fall analyst day
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Nidec as a long.

Nidec is a Japanese-listed company that dominates the global market for electric motors. It is a conglomerate.

The opportunity here is that the company had been plagued by an accounting scandal. The scandal emerged around this time last year, and progressively got worse through 2025, up to the point where they essentially pulled their financials. The most recent financials the presenter has for the company are September 2025, and they have not filed financials since then. They have provided the total revenue number and the net debt. So, you know that the company is growing revenue on a consolidated basis, and you know that they are generating real free cash flow. You do not know anything else.

Normally, that is very scary, because you do not know what is happening under the surface, and the company could be falling apart. But in this instance, the presenter thinks it is an attractive setup because approximately 20% of revenue and 40% of EBIT is exposed to the power, data center, and AI CAPEX trade. The rest of the business is more exposed to industrial, with some home appliance exposure (which the presenter acknowledges is not great), but their automotive and general industrial business, on average, are likely doing fine.

So, you have a segment of the business that is likely doing very well, and then the rest of the business is likely doing fine (but again, you do not know the numbers).

They have also quantified the amount of accounting irregularities, so you essentially know what the baseline is, adjusted for that. It ended up that they were likely overstating EBIT by 5% to 10%, and that occurred whenever there was an opportunity to understate warranties, understate provisions, understate write-offs of inventory, & bad debt (that type of stuff).

The presenter thinks you can underwrite ¥ 240 of EPS in March 2029, which would essentially be their target in a year-and-a-half. And the presenter thinks that can trade at 18x to 20x EPS, because the whole company is going to be growing earnings in the teens to 20%, mostly due to the power data center part. Then they are also taking costs out of the remainder of the business. That would take the presenter to a ¥ 4,300 yen stock price from ¥ 2,600 today, which would equate to 60% to 80% upside from here in a year-and-a-half.

The catalysts for that occurring are that they are likely going to give investors a financial update by the end of September, and then they are going to host an Analyst Day in the fall.

In the presenter’s opinion, they are already talking about the company having a “good company, bad company” dynamic. They could break up the good part from the bad. The presenter does not think you really need them to do so, because they think the earnings growth on a consolidated basis will be very strong and can support a high-teens earnings multiple. But there is optionality on that front.

[2026-06-30] On 06/25 we hosted a TMT short idea forum where investors discussed ABNB Short, EBAY Short, NYT Short, RCI Short, SPHR Short and UBER Short.

[2026-06-30] UBER has quietly ended its partnership with Waymo in Phoenix as the companies increasingly start to compete with one another.

[2026-06-30] We just recently had UBER Short discussed on the basis that autonomous vehicles will erode its value prop and cut into market share.

[2026-07-05] On the idea side, we had new TMT shorts that included ABNB Short, EBAY Short, NYT Short, RCI Short, SPHR Short and UBER Short, as well as some ideas from a recent hardware/semis dinner that included ASML, AVGO, ENTG, MU, 285A JP and 6361 JP and can be found on the Portal.

[2026-07-05] This past week we led out with some new shorts from a TMT forum where investors shared thoughts on ABNB Short, EBAY Short, NYT Short, RCI Short, SPHR Short and UBER Short.

ideas.th: Dead-app traffic falling double digits yearly; Thumbtack and Meta AI competition, heavy marketing spend and cash-draining acquisition threaten buyback support
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Yelp as a short.

Yelp is trading at $22 per share and has a $1.2 billion market cap. Eight million shares are short out of the 59 million outstanding.

Revenue base is ~$1.4 billion, and they generate approximately $350 million in EBITDA. As a comparison, pre-COVID (2019), the revenue base was $900 million and EBITDA was approximately $200 million.

In the presenter’s view, it is unclear that people are still using that app. Everyone has it on their phone, but it is likely one of those dead apps. The traffic patterns have continued deteriorating at a double-digit decline every year over the last three years. The presenter believes that continues.

Competitive intensity is worsening. There is a private company called Thumbtack, that the presenter recently met with. They are generating approximately $500 million in revenue. The presenter believes they have a phenomenal management team. If there is a survivor in this category, the presenter believes that is going to be it, because they are doing things that are very different. They do not advertise, and they still grow modestly. Yelp, on the other hand, is spending close to a third of its money advertising. That is why the EBITDA flow-through from $1.4 billion is only $350 million. They spend about $600 million in marketing and sales.

The competition is only getting worse.

The presenter thinks there is a small, tiny company that many people might be using, which is called Belly. It is starting to gain traction especially in the younger demographic. The other big entry that is going to get much more serious over time is Meta. If you think about how you use Belly or Yelp, Meta is starting to take all the consumer information, content, all the likes, dislikes, etc., and starting to expose that within its app. The presenter believes Meta AI is going to be the best app in this space, because it is going to have the best data. From a competitive perspective, Yelp is simply in the wrong place.

In terms of the business, it is a founder-run company. The CFO has been there for five years.

He is the fourth CFO since the company went public in 2011. Most recently, they did an acquisition in the beginning of the year. They bought a middleman distributor, a company that facilitates buying of advertising online. In the presenter’s opinion, it is a little bit of self-dealing, in order to keep the numbers going. In order to finalize the acquisition, they spent $300 million, and they wiped out all their cash. So now they are finally cash and debt even.

They had always been a cash-rich company, which enabled them to keep buying back stock.

They are continuing the share buyback, but the cash and debt is about the same, so now the risk profile has gone up significantly. In terms of the setup, the way that they guide, they always beat the quarter by a little bit, so the stock generally trades up into the print, and then gives up those gains. The presenter thinks you are waiting for that quarter where the traffic pattern continues to deteriorate so much that they cannot come back from it. And then at that point, the balance sheet looks rather precarious and they cannot sustain the buyback at that time. When / if that occurs, the presenter believes there is tremendous downside (around 50%). And once this thing goes down, the presenter is not sure there is much left to the story.
