ideas.th: Paramount deal risk-arb spread: state AGs leaning against suing, no substantive antitrust issue, upbeat EU meetings, ticking fee and break fee protect downside
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss the Warner Brothers risk-arb spread.

For context, Nexstar and Tegna closed; that was a highly contentious deal. Live Nation, the presenter personally has done work there and did not think there was an issue. The states challenged that. They brought it to a jury trial, not likely due to a legal issue, but because it is an emotional issue for consumers.

On the back of those two cases, the market / investors became nervous that the state AGs could choose to sue Paramount's potential acquisition of Warner Brothers. There are several issues that are different. The presenter does not think there is a real substantive antitrust issue. The presenter thinks the issue that the arb community thinks is the most credible is the movie studio issue, but the presenter do es not think there is an issue there. The presenter does not think that Paramount Skydance can be sued with a jury trial, because you need damages for that to occur.

There has been recent reporting. The state AGs did this big press conference recently touting their wins. They were asked about Paramount and Warner Brothers, and they did not really comment. Then, the re has been recent reporting from an intelligence platform that says that the state AGs are leaning toward not suing the transaction.

The presenter met with management from Paramount recently and that was the impression that they got as well. The presenter thinks David Ellison was in Europe over the last two weeks meeting with the regulators there. They sound relatively upbeat around the regulatory picture. The presenter thinks the consensus is 2025 to 2026 if this gets sued by the states, it would obviously drag the transaction out, but there is a ticking fee.

The presenter thinks over time, the downside is going to improve because the company is going to deleverage. There is a big term fee that is going to help your downside. The presenter thinks there is optionality from Netflix to come back if a transaction were not to occur.

In summary, management sounds good. Reporting is trending in the right direction. The presenter does not think there is a legal basis. The presenter thinks the states have max leverage at the moment — not when they file a suit — and then they will settle for job concessions, so on and so forth.

ideas.th: Post-aerospace sale, $900M net cash is most of the $1.4B cap; RemainCo packaging at ~5x EBITDA vs Silgan 8x with cost-outs lifting EBITDA >$100M
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss TriMas as a long.

TriMas designs and manufactures a broad range of packaging products. Eighty percent of revenue consists of dispensers, caps, and things of that nature that go into beauty care and food & beverage. Twenty percent goes into industrial end markets. These are closures for drums for hazardous materials, etc. It is not the fastest growing business, but the presenter would describe it as a decent collection of assets.

Historically, the company was a “mini” conglomerate. They have been selling assets over time. The simplification is essentially complete now. They sold their aerospace fastener business (that deal closed in March). It is a $1.4 billion market cap, a $500 million EV. They have $900 million of net cash. The vast majority of their market cap is in cash. Trailing EBITDA is $85 million.

There are two factors that should improve EBITDA. First, there are some stranded costs that they are going to get rid of, as well as additional self-help initiatives to help improve the margin profile. The presenter thinks they can get EBITDA to over $100 million. The RemainCo is currently trading at approximately 5x EV/EBITDA. You have a pro forma EV of $500 million, trailing EBITDA of approximately $85 million, and then there is ~$25 million of cost-outs, both through some stranded corporate, and then a continuation of self-help initiatives previously described.

In terms of the comp set, the presenter believes the closest peer is Silgan (ticker: SLGN). They have a very similar businesses but Silgan trades at 8x EV/EBITDA. Aptar is another comp, but they have a nice health care business, so you need to make some assumptions around what that is worth. They kind of look at it as sub-5x versus 8x. The question is, what are they going to do with the capital. The presenter thinks the most likely outcome is that they buy back a third of the company (or something to that effect), and then do M&A with the balance.

You can run scenarios on what you think they are going to do. The presenter does not think it is heroic for the stock to trade in the mid - $50s (it is currently trading at $38). The presenter likes the management team and thinks they have been prudent about selling assets. The presenter does not think they are going to do transformational M&A (they will likely do several small to mid-sized deals, or maybe one medium-sized deal).

ideas.th: Post-spin conglomerate at <9x EBITDA; two-year spin anniversary passed and activist pushing sale of dental or health IT, each worth more than the whole
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Solventum as a long.

Solventum has a $13 billion market cap, with $4.5 billion of debt, generating $2 billion of EBITDA, trading at just under 9x. This business is a classic sum-of-the-parts story. When this business first spun out, there were four businesses. One is called med-surg, which is a wound management system. Second is the dental business, which consists mainly of a fillers and braces business. The third business is healthcare revenue cycle management business for hospitals, i.e. the coding business. The fourth business is the filtration business.

It does not take a genius to figure out that none of these businesses belong with each other.

The plan is to sell the other three and keep med-surg, the core wound business. They sold the filtration business, which is the worst business of the four, for 23x EBITDA to Thermo Fisher last year. Since then, management has been very reticent about selling more business units before the 2-year spin anniversary notwithstanding what happened with Kellanova. The 2-year anniversary just passed and an activist fund is demanding they do more assets ales. So, the presenter thinks there should be an opening.

April 1st was the two-year anniversary and the presenter believes they sell either dental or HIS. There is an activist firm that has been writing letters demanding that they sell one or two business segments. Every single segment as a standalone business should trade higher than 9x; so, no matter what they sell, it is going to be a massive upgrade.

If you do an ultra-conservative sum-of-the-parts math, and put 10x on med-surg business, 11x on the dental business (all below peers), and 15x on the healthcare IT business, the presenter’s price target is $100 per share.

ideas.th: Accretive CNL Healthcare merger gives scale and deleveraging; same senior-housing supply/demand tailwinds plus understated synergies and tuck-in M&A
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Sonida Senior Living (market cap: $1.7 billion) as a long.

Similar to the Brookdale Senior Living thesis, there is very favorable supply-demand dynamics over the coming years. Sonida had a troubled history, as the whole industry did, dealing with COVID, as well as oversupply and liquidity issues. A real estate fund has been financing it for the last five years. They just put in the first $100 million, and now they own a third of the company.

What got the presenter really excited about the story is that they closed a transformational merger that was massively accretive with a private REIT called CNL Healthcare. That deal closed in late March. It gave them a solid national footprint, they de-levered, and it made them the eighth largest player. The company is still smaller than Brookdale, but all the similar trends that were spoken about earlier, apply to Sonida such as occupancy gains and rent growth.

What is unique to them is, over the last 2+ years they bought low-occupancy / weak assets.

Then, they put them on their platform, and they got occupancy up m eaningfully. They achieved double-digit attractive yields on those deals. They are still going to be a consolidator, and they have capacity to do additional tuck-in deals.

Similar to Brookdale, but unlike Ventas and Welltower, they are a C-Corp and they are recycling capital. The chairman and the CEO wrote a joint letter to shareholders about a month ago introducing a capital allocation framework, and how they are measuring deals and value creation. It is not something you see that often anymore.

Then on the synergies, the presenter thinks they are understated. It is covered by REIT analysts and healthcare analysts, the numbers are pretty messy, and they are slow to update.

New coverage is rolling out as the company closed th is deal. But basically, the $16 to $20 million synergy target, it is a day one number, then they have management fees that they are internalizing, and they have other advisory fees. If you give them credit for this, that could be another 10% upside to EBITDA.

The presenter thinks that they should compound EBITDA in mid-teens. At roughly 15x the presenter’s 2026 EBITDA estimate and an 8% cap rate, Sonida does not reflect its improved scale, capital access, and longer runway for organic and inorganic growth. The presenter thinks the upside is approximately 33% to 49%. Management is also very well-incentivized.

They are really accessible. The CIO from the company is from the fund that controls a third of the company. They are really well incentivized with PSUs. They own 100% of the real estate. Liquidity also improved meaningfully (it historically traded $2 million per day, and now it is trading $25 million per day). The presenter thinks later in the year, they will start using more [FFO] metrics and similar REIT metrics. The night of the idea dinner the company filed an ATM, which they said they would do on an opportunistic basis for additional tuck-in M&A. The stock has traded decently since the merger, and the presenter feels in a world with a lot of AI disruption, Sonida has really good trends over the next few years.

ideas.co: Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority Bonds
ideas.th: PREPA bonds at $0.72: oversight board turnover, first rate increase since 2015 and admin-expense litigation point to $0.90-0.95 settlement within ~12 months
ideas.cat: Oversight board replacement; PREB rate rider; First Circuit ruling
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss the Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority bonds as a long (PR PRCPWR 5.25% 07/01/2023 Muni).

In terms of the setup, this is a distressed municipal restructuring in Puerto Rico (an $8.5 billion debt stack that trades very liquid). For background, PREPA has been in bankruptcy since 2017 but there have been a few recent events to lead the presenter to believe that an emergence from bankruptcy may well occur in the next 12 months. The PREPA bonds are currently trading at approximately $0.72, and they trade in a very liquid manner across multiple CUSIP s. They are a holder of Co-Op bonds, but it is trading in a very liquid manner and nearly all holders have joined the Co-Op. The presenter thinks, based on public information, that you can get to a deal where you negotiate an outcome of $0.90 to $0.95 in approximately 12 months, and the bankruptcy process can recovery $1.40 over a multi-year period.

If you go back to 2015, Puerto Rico declared its debt unpayable. Then in 2017, Hurricane Maria devastated the island and PREPA ultimately entered a bankruptcy process knows as Title III. The PREP A bonds are currently trading at $0.7 2, and there have been several attempts to get a deal done since 2019. Several deals have been on the table for approximately $0.80, which ultimately fell apart. In the presenter’s opinion, the reason the deal fell apart was bad incentives. The groups would get very close to a deal, but the terms would ultimately fall apart. Importantly, the islands economic position is much stronger today, boosting a growing workforce and 5.6% unemployment rate, down from over 8% in 2021, making it easier for all parties to get to a win-win outcome.

Then in August of last year, President Trump finally removed six of the seven members of the oversight board. It is stuck in litigation at the moment, but the presenter thinks the majority of seven members will ultimately get replaced with new members on the oversight board, and then you get to a restructuring at $0.90 to $0.95 cents to the dollar. There is a cliff on it too, or a fuse, which the presenter believes is good because all of the legacy holdovers have terms that expire in the summer of 2027. The presenter thinks you are likely to get to a deal by 2027, and that is when it all of this comes to a head. That is the first point, an improving political backdrop.

The second catalyst to the thesis is that Puerto Rico’s electricity rate regulator, the PREB (Puerto Rico Energy Bureau), recently offered an approximate two-cent rate increase on their electricity rates with a “placeholder” for a debt rider. PREPA had not raised electric rates since 2015. This helped rerate the bonds from $0.66 to $0.72. For context, the presenter believes that each 1c/kwh that the receive a rate increase on is worth approximately $0.20 to $0.25 to the bonds, so that was a potential 40 to 50-point uplift on the rate increase alone. The third factor relates to the bankruptcy process that is ongoing. It has been a contentious litigation situation. There is a separate process in the First Circuit right now where there is an administrative expense claim that is being reviewed, and that is pursuing par plus accrued on the bonds. The bonds are $0.72 on par currently excluding accrued interest. The accrued or the unpaid is ~$0.45. If they win on the bankruptcy litigation, then you get ~$1.45. That is three years out but the presenter believes you will see settlement announcements coming in at $0.90 or $0.95 in approximately one year.

So, what is the downside? The presenter thinks that if this situation remains in stasis, and if you have bad political incentives in place, the bear case is as low as $0.60. But the real issue on the island of Puerto Rico is to improve the power grid. There is a big CAPEX initiative to reinvigorate the ir grid and resolving the bankruptcy helps achieve that outcome.

The presenter thinks it is a very straightforward story. The bonds are at $0.72. Base case, you are getting $0.90 to $0.95 in approximately one year. If bondholders pursue the litigation with a multi-year strategy on the Administrative Expense claim, the presenter is part of that group — this is all public information — the presenter thinks you can realize total value of $1.40 or more over roughly three years. And if they are in stasis, the downside is $0.60.

ideas.th: Clean Earth sale cleared; $14.50-16.50 special dividend leaves RemainCo stub at ~4x EBITDA (2.5x 2027) vs peers 7-8x, rail drag ending; high short interest
ideas.cat: Deal close end of May; dividend announcement
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Enviri as a long.

The presenter thinks this is one of the most compelling situations they have seen in a long time. There are 88 million fully diluted shares outstanding at $19.50 per share, which equates to a $1.8 billion market cap. For reference, they have $1.6 billion in debt, which equates to a $3.2 billion EV.

The company sold a division to Veolia, so they are bringing in a significant amount of cash — the presenter thinks it is $3 billion — and what they are going to do is pay a dividend. They have given a range of $14.50 to $16.50 on the dividend that they are going to pay to shareholders. Obviously, if you are at the top end of that range at $16.50 against a $19.50 stock, then you are buying the stu bat $3. If you are at the low end, you are buying the stub at $5.

In either of those situations, you are buying the RemainCo at approximately 4x EV/EBITDA.

For reference, a ll of the public comps trade between 7x and 8x EV/EBITDA. What is interesting about this situation is, the business they sold, they sold at 18.8x EV/EBITDA. The presenter believes the se two remaining businesses are worth at least 7x EV/EBITDA.

The two business segments that you are left with are Harsco Environmental Services and Harsco Rail. Harsco Rail has been the anchor around this company. Right before COVID, they entered into “engineered-to-order” contracts, which were essentially take-or-pay contracts where they, as the builder of these rail devices, ate all the overage. And the overages were material.

So net-net, this stock has been draining free cash, because they have been paying out to their customers for the last four years. The company says they are going to stop it. The reason why the presenter thinks it is interesting is the deal has been cleared. It looks like this deal is going to be going through by the end of May. The only information they have not released is what the dividend is going to be. They said they are going to give that update five days before closure, so that will likely be at the end of this month. In terms of the dividend, investors are getting $14.50 to $16.50. If you are getting $15.50, for arguments sake, they have guided to $140 million of EBITDA, which is $170 million from environmental solutions, and approximately a $20 million negative contribution from rail. A t the current price, you are buying the RemainCo at ~4x EBITDA. If you assume normal growth in 2027, the presenter believes you are buying it closer to 2.5x.

They are paying off almost all the debt. They are cleaning out the existing debt, and then they said they are going to borrow up to 2x EBITDA. Let us call it $280 million. So, the presenter thinks that is the math to use: 88 million fully diluted shares, $280 million. You have $4 per share in the stub today. If you use a 6x multiple, you get closer to $8 per share in value for the stub. If you assume a 7.5x multiple on 2027, you get to $12 in value for the stub.

The presenter thinks this is an interesting setup. If you do any work, you will notice there is larger than normal short interest, relatively speaking. There are 81 million shares outstanding (on a notional basis); the rest are simply RSUs, SARs, and PSUs. There are 81 million shares outstanding with 12 million of those shares sold short. The short interest is material and is a factor in why this is a long right now.

ideas.th: DOGE fears overdone: federal business +8%, 16% FCF yield, $400M buyback; VA medical exam contract renewal in October clears the main overhang
ideas.cat: VA contract renewal (Oct); OBBB eligibility redeterminations
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Maximus as a long.

Maximus has a $3.1 billion market cap and the stock is fairly liquid (it trades $50 million ADV).

It is a government consultant in the age of DOGE, where competitors like Booz Allen are down 40% over the course of one year. For context, MMS is down 30% year to date. But for MMS, despite all headline risk, their federal business is up 8% year-over-year, so they have actually been winning on the operational front.

It is currently trading at 6.5x EV/EBITDA. If you add backs tock-based comp, it trades at 6x EV/EBITDA. It has a 12% trailing free cash flow yield with $372 million of trailing free cash flow. However, they have guided to $500 million of free cash flow for this year — that is a 16% free cash flow yield — because some of the AR that got postponed because of the government shutdown comes into this year.

The balance sheet is good. It is sub-2x net leverage. It is going to de-lever further to 1.5x or 1.25x levered, so the presenter believes the balance sheet is clearly not the issue.

The stock is currently trading at $59 per share and the presenter has a $171 price target a year from now (approximately 200% upside from here). The presenter believes $700 million of trailing EBITDA goes to $770 million by the end of next year and they use a 14x multiple, which is the five to ten year average for the business. Pre-DOGE, some of the other contractors would trade at a 16x to 18x multiple. You have already gotten through Q1, so the company has guided up EBITDA, operating margins, and EPS, all higher for 2026. They also put in place a $400 million buyback against a $3.1 billion market cap. They are going to likely generate $500 million of free cash flow for this year.

In terms of the setup, there is one big catalyst, and then three or four smaller catalysts. The big risk that the presenter thinks investors are worried about is, it is ~$5.2 billion of revenue, but roughly $1 billion of revenue is derived from administering VA benefits. A veteran from Oklahoma walks in and says they served in the war and they have issues with their knee.

Maximus has built out a network of 10,000 providers across the country, and they will put you in front of a doctor. That contract is a two-year renewal. They bought their way into it, but they have had this contract since 2008. There are four providers (Maximus, Leidos, i Deloitte, and UnitedHealthcare) and share is usually evenly split between these 4 players (25%, 25%, 25%, and 25%). Maximus has been doing better than these three competitors, so they may be winning 30% of the volume. The presenter believes they are outperforming currently and picking up a little share in terms of volume. The reason why the presenter has high confidence that come October, the company is going to announce the next two-year renewal at as good, if not better rates, than what they have currently — and kind of clear that overhang, is you do not need to outrun the bear. You have got to outrun the other three competitors. The presenter believes there is only one other provider who could come in and unseat the four incumbents. Again, you need to build out a network of 10,000 doctors. To be clear, they bought into the business in 2021. They have been trying to get into the business since 2008. They have grown this business from $650 million in revenue when they bought in, to approximately $1 billion of revenue.

Maximus has claimed to have the highest value-based care score of all four. They actually have the lowest price. They are outperforming their volume metrics. They have invested a lot of technology into this, which the presenter will get into. The presenter feels good that they are going to win this contract. Come October when they say they renewed another two years and margins are actually even better, that should clear any such overhang.

There are two or three other smaller catalysts that are interesting. This has been a civic / government contractor as compared to the defense peers, like the Booz Allens of the world.

However, six months ago, they won a $200 million contract from the US Air Force, which is a critical customer to have for cybersecurity consulting. The presenter believes this is a huge stamp of approval. They beat out companies like Lockheed Martin and Accenture.

In the presenter’s opinion, they also are going to start talking about their technology offering for the VA benefits. The presenter believes this company can potentially become the Palantir of medical records. For the VA benefits contract, they are processing 10 million pages of medical records per day on the Amazon cloud, and they are basically taking eight or nine different form factors. Think of literally paper medical records from the Vietnam War, and they are homogenizing — Epic, Cerner, and paper records — all of this into a uniform code.

That is how they can process these VA benefits better than anybody else. They are using AI for this. In the presenter’s opinion, on the Q1 earnings call, the reason why they bumped up operating margin by another 30 basis points for the year is because of AI. They used to have 300 people looking through X-rays in these medical forms, tagging in the PDF document where to look for that. Now with AI, they are getting better and better and they have been putting a ton of money into this. The presenter thinks the big catalyst is you renew this VA contract and shareholders breathe a sigh of relief.

The fourth catalyst is that the One Big, Beautiful Bill changed SNAP benefits, unemployment benefits, and Medicaid benefits. Maximus administers the benefits, in the sense that they make sure you are eligible for these benefits. If you reach a point where you have to redetermine eligibility 2x or 3x per year — i.e. do you have a job, are you eligible — they get paid per interaction. One touch, when it becomes three, this volume could triple, which equates to ~25% of the business. That is all upside for them. Finally, longer-term, they do the call center for Medicaid. They have a 95% satisfaction rate.

The IRS website, which has a 40% satisfaction rate, and Social Security, which has a 30% satisfaction rate, could in theory become eligible for a contract (this would be a multi-billion-dollar contract). It is sort of a right-tail situation. The presenter thinks they have become a real threat for Booz Allen, Hamilton, Leidos, and GDIT. They could get taken out on the defense side. The presenter believes Deloitte or Accenture could also be interested, but the presenter thinks Epic or Cerner might come for this technology as well.

ideas.th: Malone repeating Sunrise playbook: Ziggo Group (Ziggo+Telenet) spin worth $10-15 plus >$14.50 parent cash/investments and VMO2 fiber value
ideas.cat: Ziggo transaction close 2H26; spin next year
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Liberty Global as a long.

Liberty Global has a $4 billion market cap. It trades approximately $40 million per day across various share classes.

The presenter acknowledges that the company screens poorly. It screens as if there is $29 billion of debt on a $4 billion market cap. But when you look at the non-recourse nature of the debt, there is no debt at the parent company and a bundle of cash. This is basically a collection of cash, investments, and stakes in various European telecom assets. A classic Malone story.

What is interesting now is that he ran this exact playbook in 2023 and 2024, where they spun out Sunrise, which was a Swiss telecom asset. The stock was at $17 when Sunrise came out, and it was $10 on the stock. You essentially earned a 50% + return over that time period.

As it relates to Liberty Global, the stock is currently trading at $12 per share. The presenter thinks the transaction they are working on is spinning out Ziggo Group. That would be worth between $10 and $15 on a $12 stock. The parent company itself has over $14.50 in cash & investments.

The first transaction is the creation of the Ziggo Group. They are buying in and consolidating the other 50% of Ziggo that Vodafone owns with their own 50%, and then they are merging that with their Telenet group. This transaction creates a scaled Benelux platform that should close in the second half of this year. Then next year, the presenter believes they will spin out Ziggo Group. The presenter thinks there is somewhere north of $3 billion of EBITDA and $500 million of free cash flow. A 7% dividend yield on that gets you to $10 to $15.

While they are creating Ziggo and splitting off their Belgian assets. Telenet, which is the service assets, is going into that. Then, there is VMO2, which is essentially a fiber network that is being combined with two other assets, and the presenter thinks there are a few dollars per share of value there. That transaction will also create the biggest fiber competitor to British Telecom’s Openreach, and there should be a lot of CAPEX synergies there.

The presenter thinks this combination is when the value gets realized, and that the stock is worth between $25 to $30 when it is currently trading at $12. The catalysts are starting next year in earnest, but the Ziggo transaction kicks it all off later this year. The presenter thinks you start to have multiple catalysts ahead. The managing team has been incentivized to get this done plus John Malone is cleaning up his estate. In terms of a timeline, the presenter thinks this occurs over the next 18 months.

ideas.th: Accounting restatement (<2% revenue) and AI overhang mask improving CRO demand from $300B patent cliff and new management reversing share loss
ideas.cat: Restated financials within ~2 weeks; book-to-bill; activist/PE interest
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss ICON plc as a long.

Broadly speaking, from a special situation perspective, the presenter thinks there is a lot to do right now with in health care. The presenter happens to be involved in a handful of healthcare stocks that happen to have an activist presence.

The idea that the presenter would like to discuss does not have an activist yet. It is a CRO. In terms of the setup, before the emergence of AI, the stock traded between $250 and $300.

When the AI threat emerged, it traded between $200 and $250. Then, the company faced an accounting issue, so the stock is now trading at $110.

The accounting issue is — and management has spoken to investors, so they are pretty open about it at this point — there was a group inside one of their divisions that effectively was accelerating revenue recognition before performing the services. They have quantified that at less than 2% of total revenue for 2023 and 2024. Ironically, that likely pushes that revenue into 2025 and 2026. They have come out as recently as last week and said that they will file all of their statements within two weeks from last Friday. The presenter thinks that they are going to file those financial statements soon.

The core thesis here is that the underlying CRO business is improving. The presenter thinks there are two drivers over the next two years. One is that there is a $300 billion patent cliff for pharma between 2028 and 2031, which is effectively 40% of all pharma revenue. If you do some back of the envelope math on how much the presenter thinks they need to spend to replace that, it implies revenue acceleration within the CROs from low single digits to high single digits.

The second driver to the thesis is specific to ICON, which is a new management team. They have been losing share for two years. A lot of investors have done a lot of work to figure out why that was the case. Some of the presenter’s survey data suggests that that has bottomed and in fact has reversed. There are a handful of different reasons around that, but what they are providing to the customer is really resonating, in the presenter’s opinion.

Ultimately, the presenter thinks the stock is depressed because of the accounting issue and because of this AI overhang. The presenter thinks that they are going to file their financials in the next two weeks. The presenter believes that they are going to have the best book-to-bill in the whole industry when they file. Once that happens, the presenter thinks that unlocks value, and then you start to see over the next two years their book-to-bill bottom at 1 and get back to 1.2 The presenter thinks they are 30% to 35% above the Street on EBITDA two and a half years out, and 50% to 60% above the Street on EPS two and a half years out. Ultimately, the presenter thinks the stock will trade back to $200 to $250. Then, from an activist angle, the presenter believes that there are some private equity firms that could be interested.

ideas.th: Next bitcoin miner to sign a hyperscaler AI lease: ~500MW deal with three interested parties would create $3-4B value on $1.1B equity
ideas.cat: Hyperscaler lease announcement in coming months
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Core Scientific as a long.

The presenter believes Core Scientific can be the next bitcoin miner to have a material move on a deal. Obviously, you had Hut 8 do a deal earlier this year. Then Terawulf raised equity and said a deal is forthcoming, and that stock is up a lot (the presenter thinks that deal is priced in to Terawulf’s shares at this point).

But the stock that the presenter thinks is not priced in is Core Scientific. Core Scientific was the first Bitcoin miner to convert their power use to AI, but it is a little bit different than the others, because they did a 590 megawatt deal with CoreWeave. CoreWeave is a neo-cloud, with a big bull/bear debate on what its real moat is. But for Core Scientific, it is an amazing deal, where CoreWeave is paying them over a period of five or six years to essentially finance all the equipment and PP&E. It was an unencumbered, amazing asset that is on Core Scientific’s balance sheet, but the market was nervous regarding CoreWeave as a customer.

If you fast forward to where we are today, Anthropic is doing amazing. Everybody knows that demand is materially higher than what investors had thought. There are more use cases.

All the Bitcoin miners are signing deals. Core Scientific has exclusivity to negotiate 500 mwh of power across two sites with a hyperscaler. That exclusivity period expired per their recent earnings call. The prevailing opinion, based on what the presenter has been hearing when people talk about the stock, is there is nothing wrong with the sites but that the team that was working on the deal changed firms and it is possible they are working on the deal at a different hyperscaler already.

What Core Scientific said publicly is that they have three interested parties. In terms of how much power they have to sell, t they have one gigawatt that is available over the next 12 to 18 months, and the size of this was expected to be approximately 500 megawatts. They have two sites that have approximately 500 megawatts available, but with some expansion options, so the presenter thinks this encompassed two sites.

If you assume $11 per megawatt multiplied by 500 megawatts, that equates to $5.5 billion (80% project financing / 20% equity). The company recently raised $3.3 billion of debt that was secured by the CoreWeave contract (discussed earlier), and they are using $2.2 billion of those proceeds to be the equity for the next gigawatt. Of this $5.5 billion, they would have $4.4 billion of debt and $1.1 billion of equity. Generally, you get a 15% average cash yield on the $5.5 billion (it will increase each year, but the average is 15%). They will convert that into NOI at 80% (so only 20% of annual payment will be absorbing costs). You are looking at $600 million of annual cash flow that would grow with inflation escalators. At a 6% cap rate, that would be worth $3 to $4 billion of value versus the $1.1 that they are putting up. If you give it a cheaper multiple on the CoreWeave part of the contract, the presenter believes it would move the stock from $23 to $30. If they were to do another 500 megawatt deal, which the presenter believes can be accomplished later this year or early next year, that would move the stock to $35 to $38 in their opinion.

The presenter thought it was interesting at a recent industry conference to have various panelists talk about the human capital that CoreWeave, Nebius, and various other neoc louds have. It gives the presenter more confidence today that these neoc louds have a real role, because they seem to be learning how to work with all of this infrastructure faster and better than others. The presenter thinks it is not a big leap of faith to bet on this today. This is a $23 stock that could be worth $30 or $35. Based on the way management talks, the presenter thinks investors should get an announcement in the next couple of months.

ideas.th: Montana Renewables SAF ramp coincides with RVO hike (RINs $0.50 to $2.08), ~$3/gal margins could yield $375-450M EBITDA on first 150M gallons; takeout candidate
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Calumet as a long.

Calumet has a $2.8 billion market cap. In terms of the setup, this is one of those situations where you have a lot of events coming over the next three months, and then you have a lot of potential catalysts coming over the next 18 months. The presenter thinks this company will ultimately be taken out before the end of 2028.

In terms of the business, they have two refineries. They have one traditional refinery in Shreveport, Louisiana. About a third of their production is specialty waxes, paraffins, etc., while the remaining production is mostly basic fuels and asphalt. That business (specialty chemicals) is doing very well at the moment because of the war in Iran.

Then they have a small business called Performance Brands, which consists of higher end motor oils. To give you a sense of the quality of that business, last year Calumet announced it had entered into a definitive agreement to sell assets related to the industrial portion of its Royal Purple business (a high-quality motor oil) for $110 million or 10x EBITDA. The rest of Performance Brands is likely going to generate approximately $60 million of EBITDA this year. If you value that at 10x, it equates to ~$600 million.

If you value the rest of the traditional refinery business at 4x, the presenter uses a conservative number of approximately $200 million of EBITDA, although they believe the real number is going to be closer to $300 million. That is their traditional business.

What gets investors excited about this story is that they have a refinery in Montana that is going to be one of the largest suppliers of sustainable air fuel. They received DOE financing at approximately 4.5% over 15 years to build out their sustainable air fuel capacity at Montana Renewables. It is going to be done in two phases. They promised 300 million gallons. The first 150 million gallons came online beginning in May 2026.

For those investors who do not follow renewable diesel or sustainable air fuels, a lot of it is based on what the EPA determines are “renewable volume obligations.” The EPA made a mistake in 2024 and 2025 and had renewable volume obligations at 3.5 billion gallons for the country. They just renewed it for 2026 to 2027. It is 5.6 billion gallons (a huge step increase).

So RINs, which are Renewable Identification Numbers, have gone from $0.50 to $2.08 in three months. Renewable diesel prices have gone from $0.75 per gallon to $2.40. Th is company is signing offtake agreements for the full 150 million gallons that just came online at a $1 to $2 premium to renewable diesel. With that being said, the presenter believes that this company should be earning ~$3 per gallon on 150 million gallons (and that is backing out their cost). All of a sudden, you have this plant that on the first half of its production is going to be generating $450 million of EBITDA. The company says the second half of the 150 million gallons will be coming online, potentially, in the first half of 2027. The presenter is assuming it occurs in the back half of 2027. This is a business that has potential to generate upwards of $1 billion of EBITDA.

By the way, that 150 million gallons is based on a 65% yield. The presenter believes that they are going to be running at a 90% yield. By doing that, you take 150 million gallons and bring them over 200 million very quickly. Ultimately, if they start getting 400 million gallons at $3 per gallon, you are well north of $1 billion.

They have offtake agreements. They have publicly disclosed about 110 million gallons of the 150 million that are first coming out. The presenter is un sure as to why they have not disclosed the other part, but the presenter believes it is all sold out. On the first 150 million gallons, if you put 150 million gallons at $3 per gallon — but let us haircut that and say $2.75 or $2.50 per gallon — you get somewhere around $375 million. Using a 9x or 10x multiple on that, back out debt, and then there is ~14% minority interest, you get to $3 billion just for the first 150 million gallons. Then if you discount the second half aggressively, you are at $2 billion for Montana Renewables. That would equate to a $60 stock price versus a current stock price of $32.

Montana Renewables is coming online this quarter. The presenter thinks they are going to disclose all the other offtake agreements. They are going to start talking about the next 150 million gallons. Again, the presenter thinks that will actually end up being 200 million gallons. And then, as the presenter said, they think this is probably an asset that someone like Shell — which is part of the offtake agreement pool for the first 150 million gallons — would be interested in acquiring.

ideas.th: Exited weak leases; 80+ cohort demand +9%/yr vs ~1% supply drives high-single-digit pricing and 60-70% incrementals above 85% occupancy; Q1 dip was weather/flu
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Brookdale Senior Living as a long.

BKD has a $3 billion market cap and a ~$7 billion EV.

BKD is a private pay senior housing operator, one of the largest, that just offloaded an underperforming lease portfolio. The company is now 75% owned and operated properties, a much better occupancy profile, and a decade-wide demand acceleration tailwind driven by the silver wave of baby boomers turning 80+. Starting this year, there are twice as many 80+ - year-olds joining that cohort every year for the next ten years, and that leads to TAM growth of 9%. At the same time, there is only 1% supply growth per year given current interest rates, construction costs, labor costs, etc. Essentially, you cannot price a new project with attractive returns against the established operators.

What that leads to is high single digit revenue growth. They just put through a high single digit price hike this year (which stuck). That should lead to double digit EBITDA growth.

That leads the presenter to model approximately $620 million in EBITDA for next year. The presenter believes that the Street is too low because they have not remodeled based on the new core portfolio. For reference, the Street is at $575 million.

If this is a tailwind that is occurring over the next decade with no supply growth, and the comps trade up here, the presenter believes BKD should trade with a high teens EBITDA multiple. If you put 15x to 18x on $620 million, you are looking at a $22 to $30 price target versus a current stock price of $13.

In terms of the setup, this story starts to look a lot cleaner in the back half of this year. The stock was at $17 post the Investor Day, when they laid out this growth and profitability algorithm. Then you had a few things occur. First, occupancy broke trend in Q1 of this year.

You couple that with the sell-off and inflationary fears due to the war in Iran, which caused the stock to trade off.

On the occupancy aspect, given normal seasonality, occupancy is usually down 20-ish basis points during this period; so, the 30 basis points was a little bit above norm. That being said, you had two massive winter storms in January and February plus an elevated flu season.

You look to April occupancy growth, which is back on track, and the presenter thinks they are about to move into the summer “move-in” season.

The presenter thinks the market overreacted. As this profile moves forward and you get above 85% occupancy, it is 60% to 70% incremental margins. You look at some of the operators who are above this 85% occupancy band, they are already proving out that financial model. The presenter thinks BKD is one year behind it, trading at a discount for that reason.

[2026-05-10] I don’t have too much extra to add on this one, but I think the company likely will continue to grind higher as it executes from here.

ideas.th: 'Mini-Siemens Energy': modular reciprocating gas engines for data centers (1.6GW booked, ~18-month lead time) hidden by sell-side; Gas Solutions divestiture
ideas.cat: Q2 Gas Solutions sale; segment reclassification; new hyperscaler deals
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Wartsila as a long.

Wartsila is a Finnish renewable energy company (with a US listed ADR) that focuses on medium-speed reciprocating gas engines (not gas turbines — this is the core differentiation vs. the aeroderivative/combined-cycle competition).

In terms of the setup, the presenter would describe it as a mini-Siemens Energy. They are divesting a business (Gas Solutions) in Q2 2026 that was hurting their margin profile and their growth rate. What remains is the core Marine and Energy franchise, where the company is repurposing its marine-engine platform — analogous to Solaris Energy Infrastructure’s mobile power pivot — into modular reciprocating gas engines (50SG, 34SG) which will then be sold to data centers.

Th is data center business was launched in earnest over the last two years. The modular architecture allows rapid scale, and cuts lead time from three-to-four years down to ~18 months vs. gas turbines.

Important to note, cumulative US data center orders booked have now crossed 1.6 GW.

Manufacturing capacity is being expanded via the Sustainable Technology Hub in Vaasa, which the presenter thinks is commissioning in Q1 2028. Customer demand visibility extends into 2029 – 2030 and the presenter believes the contracted data center revenue stream builds to ~$1.4 billion by 2030.

This month, the company announced two new hyperscaler / data-center deals in Ohio & Texas. The presenter thinks we will hear more about those deals on the earnings call that will likely cause the stock to re-rate.

In terms of the analyst coverage, most on the Street are Sell-rated or Neutral, but the presenter believes they are not looking at the growth of the data center segment. The company is expected to reclassify the energy segment the way Siemens did, which should make the data center ramp more visible to the Street within the next 12 months.

In terms of a target price, the presenter believes there is ~50% upside from current levels.

ideas.th: Power semi supply tighter than believed (TSMC/China exits, Nexperia turmoil, Japan consolidation); new 300mm fab gives 70% incrementals, EPS $3 vs $1.20
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Vishay as a long.

It is a power semiconductor company, described as a smaller version of Texas Instruments or Infineon. It has a $4 billion market cap and trades $50 to $100 million per day. The stock is currently trading at $28 per share but the presenter thinks it is worth $60 per share over the next nine months.

For background, Vishay was family-run for many years and had under-invested in the business during this time with little distribution. A professional management team was brought in five years ago, who increased CAPEX investments, bought a 300-millimeter factory, and invested in distribution.

In terms of power semiconductors, investors ’ general view is that demand is good (both cyclically and because of AI). That is all true. The presenter’s differentiation is that supply is materially lower than investors believe. There are only three companies in the world of power semiconductors that have been investing over the last five years during the down cycle: Texas Instruments, Infineon, and Vishay. In an upcycle, the presenter believes that you want to own companies with fabs that have high incremental margins. That is Vishay.

Turning to the supply side, supply for power semis is oddly very low. Cyclically, post the COVID hangover, companies have been under-investing. The second factor, in the presenter’s opinion, TSM is de-emphasizing their trailing edge foundry to focus on CoWoS (Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate). China, which was supposedly going to hurt this market, has also started to use their trailing edge fabs for back end, for DRAM, etc. So, you have reductions in supply from both TSM and China.

One other point on supply. One of their largest competitors is Nexperia. Nexperia is a Dutch-headquartered semiconductor manufacturer that got taken over by a Chinese based company in 2019, but the presenter believes it is now effectively in a civil war with itself.

According to press reports, the European parent just cut them of f from ERP access and Microsoft Office access. The presenter thinks a ll of their Western customers are likely coming to companies like Vishay saying they are sole sourced from this Chinese company and would love to pay up for non-Chinese made parts. Important to note, the fab has 70% incremental margins.

Also worth noting, it has been reported in the press that there could be consolidation in Japan. Three of the Japanese power semi companies, according to sell side reports, are merging, leading to further consolidation. So you have low supply from CAPEX, three exogenous factors reducing supply and consolidation, all in a massive up-cycle with in power semis. In terms of EPS, The Street is at ~$1.20 next year. The presenter thinks they can generate $3.00 of EPS. If that happens, the presenter believes it will trade at 20x, because it is growing double digits. So, you are looking at a $60 stock versus $27 today. The presenter thinks there are only a few analysts who cover it on the sell-side, so it is undiscovered.

Two final points: First, beyond their core business in power discrete and M OSFET s, they also have a passive business. This competes with companies like Yageo and Murata (which is one of the hottest subsectors in Asia currently as AI servers use more power and therefore need more passives to regulate that electricity). Second, everyone is raising prices. From published sell-side reports and Twitter, it appears as if all their competitors (across Vishay’s business) are raising prices. Not only do you get the incremental margins, but you also get price increases.

ideas.th: HDD duopoly: AI exabyte demand +40% vs supply +30% drives first-ever sustained pricing gains plus HAMR cost declines; 2028 EPS $70 vs $30 Street
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Seagate as a long.

Seagate is a duopoly making hard disk drives with Western Digital. Over the last year, Seagate has transitioned to being mostly a cloud business (the consumer business that sells into laptops, etc., has basically gone to zero).

The high-level thesis is that storage is mission critical to training new AI models. If you want to have the best AI model on the market, you need more data, and you need hard drives to store the data. Seagate and Western Digital are in the middle of a multi-year up cycle caused by AI. The presenter has done checks with various data center operators, hyperscalers, etc., and, in the presenter’s opinion, essentially everyone that they have spoken to has told them that real exabyte demand is growing 40%+. Supply in the hard drive industry is only growing 30%, so there is a structural supply-demand imbalance that the presenter thinks is going to persist for the next four to five years.

The hard disk drive industry is not adding capacity, so the presenter thinks supply growth in the next few years is going to remain at 30%. Because of the supply-demand mismatch, as well as increasing NAND prices, pricing is inflecting positively for essentially the first time ever.

The financial model is simple. The presenter thinks exabytes over the next few years grow 30%. They think pricing per exabyte this year is up 10% to 15%, and next year is going to be up 20% plus. The presenter thinks 2028 pricing is going to be up double digits again. Cost per exabyte declines 15% per year because of the transition to new HD technology, specifically HAMR. The presenter thinks over the next three years, EPS is going to grow at approximately a 100% CAGR. The presenter is underwriting $70 of EPS in 2028 while The Street is at $30. Twenty times that would equate to a $1,400 stock price versus $600 today, which would be ~130% upside in two years.

ideas.th: 60% drawdown prices in DAU declines from age verification/bans; payers stable, 18+ cohort and ads growing, AI a supply tailwind; trough 4x bookings
ideas.cat: Q1 earnings Apr 30 (FY bookings reiteration); summer content
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Roblox as a long.

Roblox has a $40 billion market cap, with 140 million daily active users, and should generate over $8 + billion in annual bookings this year. It is a user-generated game platform. The stock peaked in the middle of last year a t $140 per share after they had two viral hits, but it has subsequently declined 60% on concerns regarding lap ping those tough comparison this year, regulatory issues, AI disruption, and third party data that has shown declining concurrent users on the platform.

The presenter’s view is that virtually all of this is in the stock in the mid - $50s. The thesis is that the DAUs do not really drive revenue, payers do. Important to note, less than 2% of users pay, and that cohort is actually very stable. After the 50% surge in payers in the middle of 2025, payers declined just 1% in Q4, despite DAUs rolling over due to some of the headwinds the presenter previously discussed.

So why are users declining? A lot of it is mechanical (ie the company's self-imposing age verification). Also, there are some jurisdictions that have banned Roblox outright. For example, the Russian ban imposed in December accounted for 7 million users that came off the platform, but the presenter would argue that it is clearly not a reflection of demand for the platform.

From here, the presenter thinks there are a few aspects to the story that could go right. For one, the 18 + cohort is growing more than 50%, which is 2x faster than the younger users. It monetizes a lot better. On advertising, they launched a rewarded video ad in late 2025 that the presenter thinks is driving a 10% to 15% incremental booking uplift. There has been brand interest from Nike, McDonald's, and Spotify that are on the platform.

Third, the presenter thinks AI is ultimately a tailwind. That debate is not going to be necessarily resolved in the near term, but they see Roblox as a distribution layer, similar to the Microsoft pitch in some respects. AI lowers the cost of creating games and will increase supply, and those games will still need to find an audience to be monetized. It is hard to create 140 million DAU sat scale.

The presenter would say there are a couple of call options as well. There is a JV with Tencent, so they may re-enter China, and that could be a material uplift. The other aspect to the story, that is not in numbers and could be quite helpful is seasonality. As we approach the summer season, it is seasonally a time when a lot of content comes on to the platform, because these creators know that users spike as kids get out of school. It is not ridiculous to think that there will be some new viral sensation. In the presenter’s opinion, management says you do not really need that to hit their guidance, but that would certainly be helpful. In terms of the setup, they report this Thursday, April 30th. The user data has been pretty mixed but has stabilized recently. The presenter thinks Q1 bookings are fine. Everyone knows MAUs are going to be “squishy.” Based on the presenter’s view, it is really a bookings question. To them, it is whether or not they reiterate the full year 2026 bookings number.

They gave the guidance in February. With what has happened since, the presenter would argue that the negative overhangs have not gotten worse. Users have “quasi” stabilized while U. S. users have actually inflected positively. There was some noise around an Indonesia ban, but it does not seem like that would move the needle. Even so, that might only affect $50 million of bookings for the year.

There was a new announcement recently to enhance age verification dynamics that are going to come onto the platform in June, and investors are debating whether or not that was contemplated in the original guidance. In the presenter’s opinion, it is hard to know. They tend to think this roadmap is out there. They announced the first age verification changes in January, so it has been part of their roadmap for a while now. But ultimately, the presenter believes you are looking at a stock that historically troughed at 4x bookings (where it is now). On reasonable assumptions, they can get well north of 2027 EBITDA. You can put any multiple you want at this point, and there is upside. At 20x EBITDA, it would equate to an $85 stock price. If they get some sort of a viral hit again this summer, the presenter believes the stock will be over $10 0 at that point.

Key risks to the story are: further cuts to numbers, if the age verification truly impacts payers, and if there are more regulatory issues (i.e., further geographic bans), as well as longer-term questions regarding safety and outstanding lawsuits from State AGs (although many of those cases have started to settle).

ideas.th: Infinera-boosted optical (one of two scale-across vendors with own US fab) can grow 30%+, plus routers (Nscale) and AI-RAN/6G; growth from -2% to +10%
ideas.cat: San Jose fab expansion; hyperscaler optical wins
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Nokia as a long.

Everyone knows Nokia is a smartphone loser. For what it is worth, they have not owned that business since 2014. The presenter thinks the reason why most investors do not know or care is because their organic growth since then has been negative 2%. They have been a classic European conglomerate that bought a lot of different assets and did not integrate them. They kept pushing the can down the road, and landed at negative 2% organic growth since 2014, and a stock that has been negative-1% for 20 years.

The presenter believes that with new management and an extremely lucky acquisition, that will change. In 2030, Nokia will look very different from Nokia of 2025 with negative growth. The presenter thinks it is going to accelerate to double-digit growth; a company going from-2% to +10% with earnings accelerating to the mid-20%s. That will be driven by three waves. The presenter describes them as waves, because they are going to build on each other. The first is optical. The second is switches and routers, which will begin in earnest in the second half of this year. And then, the third is AI-RAN and the 6G upgrade cycle, which is expected by the end of the decade.

If you go through them one a ta time, optical is 15% of the business. It will be 20% this year.

It will be 30% exiting 2028. They play in the data center, interconnect, and scale across markets. If you went to the OFC Conference (i.e., the optical conference), you likely realized that the only part of the networking stack where there are only two vendors talking about it is Scale A cross. In the presenter’s opinion, everything else has five different form factors and 20 companies that think they are going to win.

The presenter likes industries where there are two players and you can do due diligence. If you are right about demand, you have a right to win. Those two players are Nokia and Ciena. Nokia's optical business has two businesses inside it. First is their own old business, and then the second is their timely acquisition of Infinera that they made in 2024. They were both half the size of Ciena; so, now combined, they are the same size as Ciena.

The presenter thinks the core assertion they are making about this business is that th is business can grow 30%. The Street assumes that business grows at 15%, 15%, and 8% per year. The presenter thinks the buy-side believes their peer, Ciena, can grow 40%.

There are three assertions you need to believe in the thesis. The first is that Infinera is a good business. The presenter says that is true, because if you look at their organic growth rate before COVID, it is the same organic growth rate as Ciena. What they did is, their parent company did a bad deal. They took their 45% gross margin to 35%. They owned their own fabs, which took their gross margin to 25%. And then, as soon as the business recovered during COVID, they started selling themselves. So, they ended up at Nokia, at the perfect time for the buyer, and obviously the worst time for the seller. The presenter thinks the first assertion is th at Infinera is a good business, and they believe that.

The second point is that they are still in the early innings of market growth. An influx of data going into data centers is inflecting for the first time in a while, a nd then training across multiple data centers and moving data across data centers. To give some context, Meta is connecting two data centers 80 kilometers apart, and the market size of that is $400 to $500 million. The size of the opportunity is frankly too hard to model at the moment, because it looks too good to be true, and the presenter is trying to figure out why it should not grow 40% to 50%. And they have landed on 30%, because they think it is fair to model it that way.

Every investor is trying to estimate the size of this opportunity, but based on a couple of sources, the presenter would argue it is a $5 billion market going to $25 billion (or a 35% CAGR).

The presenter thinks the third assertion is the key one — because Ciena is already up 100% and trades at 50x P/E (the presenter does not think that market question is debated) — Is this the right vendor? And this is where going to OFC was very helpful, because every single hyperscaler they spoke with talked about the importance of having more than one vendor.

Long-haul pluggables, by definition, require a lot of interoperability. You are making these CAPEX plans five years out so you cannot be stuck to one vendor when there are only two vendors.

So, if the second vendor has supply and they do not have a bad product, they have a right to win. The presenter believes they have a real strategy. They are making these modular boxes.

They have a real team from Infinera. The person who ran that business is now the CEO of the entire organization. They are spending more on R&D now than Ciena, and they have a technical advantage with at least one of the products next year.

The last point, for investors who also cover industrials, it is really good to have your own supply and your own fabs in a supply-constrained market. They are the only Western player with a fab in San Jose, which has a second fab coming online at the end of this year. They started doing it three years ago. They got a CHIPS grant, and now it is coming online. The presenter thinks it has 20x the capacity as the last fab.

Suddenly there is an extremely supply-constrained market until 2028 at a minimum. This company will have supply, and the other company will need to get supply from someone else. All of that combined is the presenter's assertion that the optical business is going to grow at least 30% (if not more).

Quickly on the other two waves. On router switches, they have not been as good as the other two. The presenter would note that they invested in Nscale, which is now the biggest European neo-cloud. On an incremental basis on Microsoft, they are winning all of the Microsoft contracts. This company has invested in them. They are the preferred partner for routers and switches. So, when you see an Nscale announcement, you should think Nokia.

The third wave is that approximately 55% of the business is mobile networks. That is 5G.

They missed 5G entirely. They were very bad, and they still have a business there. For 6G, now they have a partnership with NVIDIA. The presenter thinks there is a right tail in the cell phone tower being a data center. That is all right tail that the presenter do es not include in their numbers, but they believe exiting the decade, it will be come a real business.

Put ting it all together, the presenter is underwriting $0.65 of EPS in calendar 2029. That is 30% above The Street. At 25x P/E, which is below the sum of the parts P/E for each of the businesses, the presenter believes that multiple is appropriate. That is a 25% IRR, from $9 per share. The risk primarily is execution. But the presenter thinks that is a perfectly fair risk to have.

The last point the presenter would make is that the story is still being discovered. At OFC, which was a month ago, their product launch had fewer investors than a single meeting with Ciena’s management team. The presenter was very surprised by this.

ideas.th: Washed-out 'AI loser' owning Office/Windows distribution layer; end of OpenAI exclusivity lets Copilot become model-agnostic as models commoditize
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Microsoft as a long with a $535 price target (or 27% upside from current levels).

The presenter believes that most investors believe that Microsoft is an AI “loser.” It is the presenter's favorite type of setup because it is very contrarian.

This has been left for dead. The Street's narrative is that they are a permanent AI loser (Copilot does not work, Claude is hurting them, software /coding is dead, structural employment concerns regarding white collar workers, etc.) The stock chart agrees. You see RSI is at 24, a long sell-off, capitulation type volume, and nobody owns it. In the presenter’s view, it is a classic washout.

Here is why the presenter thinks the Street is wrong. Microsoft does not need to own the frontier model to win here. If you own the distribution layer, which is Excel, Word, Outlook, and Windows (where AI gets monetized in the enterprised), if you use the add-in, then you know what the presenter is talking about. You are going to use Excel more than you ever did, it is simply going to be easier with a better experience.

The presenter believes they finally decided to get their act together. About a week ago, they said they are going to look at Open Claude and do stuff. The presenter thinks they had an epiphany moment where they realized Copilot is not working. Claude, they know what you are doing for add-ins. They can see the add-ins happening. Claude crushes Copilot. Copilot cannot even do anything on the sheet, but Claude can go pull the information off a presser and put it in your model. The difference is unbelievable.

The news this week — they are out of OpenAI exclusivity. Is that bad? Is that good? The presenter thinks it is a positive, because it lets Copilot become model-agnostic, route to Claude or Gemini or whatever is best for that specific task. That is the Perplexity playbook applied to enterprise software, and it de-risks OpenAI execution entirely.

There are three proof points that the presenter needs to keep working: They need Azure to keep accelerating toward 39%. They need operating margins guiding up (which they have been). And the key factor is that they want to see Copilot hitting 150 million MAUs. The last proof point being the most important in terms of showing that the product actually works.

Obviously, the risk is cloud gross margin compression. At 67% gross margin, which is the lowest it has been in three years. The presenter does not love that. But the OpenAI re-negotiation and Anthropic taking code mindshare is all noise in the presenter’s view. It does not have anything to do with coding. If they lose coders — which they should because AI is perfect for coding — since all it does is code (it programs in Python to give you the answer). There will be fewer coders, but they are not the real us ers of Excel and Word anyway, so the presenter thinks this is fairly insulated.

Bottom line is, the distribution moat is there. The models, the presenter thinks, are all going to commoditize. How many frontier models are there going to be? Two or three big mega ones, but the presenter assumes that price gets cheaper. Tokens likely get cheaper over time.

If tokens get cheaper over time and Microsoft gets their act together, it is an excellent setup from here.

ideas.th: Pulte targeting bureau pricing, bi/single-merge and AI-driven fewer credit pulls threaten mortgage monopoly; EWS gov vertical slipping; rich vs TransUnion
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Equifax as a short.

Equifax is a data analytics business with two primary assets. They have the core U.S. credit bureau, and then they have an employment and income verification business. The traditional credit bureau sells all of our credit files to lenders, insurers, and banks. They have an effective regulated monopoly within mortgage. And then EWS, which is their employment verification business, has a proprietary payroll network with almost 200 million records, which they sell to lenders, landlords, and some government agencies to verify both employment and income.

Investors own this stock because they believe it has no AI risk, and they are excited that EWS has had some growth spurts. The presenter believes both are wrong. A ta recent press conference where Bill Pulte was announcing the release of lender's choice for credit scores, the most incremental data point regarding that press release, in the presenter’s opinion, was Pulte’s comment citing that the credit bureaus are next in terms of attention because of pricing. He also called out AI risk within the core credit bureaus.

To walk through some of these points: AI risk is underappreciated. If you talk to mortgage lenders, they are very bullish on their ability to close loans much quicker. You close a loan, and 50% of the time you have half the number of credit pulls required to do that. Also, Pulte shifting his focus creates this overhang of, okay, could we go to bi-merge or single-merge, or if lenders are originating loans much quicker, can we do a single credit pull that is portable throughout the entire mortgage origination process? That can compound the problems within credit pull volumes, where you have a real left case scenario where they could be down ~80%. Not to mention the pricing implications of Pulte going to 2B or 1B. Right now, it is a regulated monopoly where they all raise price together. If you remove that, it is a lot harder to drive pricing.

The other segment is their employment verification business. Every investor is excited about the government vertical. The OB3 passed last year, in which management was very bullish on their opportunity to verify benefits.

On their most recent earnings print, they missed expectations, guided down, and then talked to pushouts from 2026 to 2027 in terms of new deals, and spoke to state budgets that were tightened. That opportunity looks materially worse. In the presenter’s opinion, there is a governmental organization that is effectively releasing open-source software that allows for this verification called EMI. It is a solution that would allow lenders and verifiers to be able to mix away from this business. There is also an AI risk within the manual verification and consumer consent. If you have AI workflows that minimize the friction of collecting all this paperwork for originations and/or rent als, it lowers the case to have this product at such a high price point.

Right now, Equifax trades at ~17x. It trades at a premium to TransUnion (its closest peer), which is currently trading at 13x, since it is perceived as a better business than EWS. They think as investors realize that this is not a great business, the first trade is multiple compression between those two. 13x $10 is $130. That would equate to approximately 30% downside.

That is before taking into account any issues within mortgage volumes or EWS. If credit pull volumes are down 20% and pricing is flat, you get to $7.00 in earnings. The presenter thinks it trades 10x or $70 per share. And then there is that real left tail case where pulls are down 80%, and you can see another 50% downside.

You simply need to connect them to the existing utility lines.

They have their first customer for five pods. It is a high-grade hyperscaler (that is unnamed the presenter believes). The presenter thinks there is going to be a deluge of demand. Ultimately, the presenter would not be surprised if in 2027 they have 100 pods and they are run-rating $150 million to $170 million of EBITDA.

In the presenter’s view, they will likely need to raise some equity capital. They have raised about $80 million in the last six months to get things off the ground and install the initial pods. They are doing a small GPU as a service deal with their pods. It will be a good return, but it is not their focus going forward. They build these at 3.5x to 4x EBITDA. If you think they are worth 8x or 10x, there is a huge equity uplift. Each pod is worth ~$0.20 to $0.30 per share, so with 100 pods, the stock should be worth $20 to $30 per share.

The CEO has a relationship with the NVIDIA team and the presenter speculated that Duos could be a good candidate for a direct investment from NVIDIA. Alternatively, the presenter thinks Duos could see a hyperscaler infuse a little bit of capital, along with a 25-pod deal.

ideas.th: Post-COVID hangover ending with device/network refresh; IT spread business benefits from cloud/AI complexity and pricing, at 13x vs 15-25x history
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss CDW as a long.

CDW has a $17 billion market cap and a $22 billion EV. It trades ~$200 million per day.

CDW is a value-added reseller. They sell IT equipment and software to businesses, governments, health care customers, etc., and they provide associated support.

After two-and-a-half years of post-COVID top-line underperformance and management over-hiring, CDW is back to growth, and their long-term growth algorithm is mid to high single-digit top-line growth and double-digit EPS growth. At the same time, forward expectations are really low. The stock is trading far below its long-term average multiples. It is at approximately 13x PE versus 15x to 25x historically.

Increasing IT complexity benefits CDW. For workloads moving to the cloud and AI implementations, CDW is a critical player in the IT ecosystem. They sit between 1,000 vendors who want access to CDW's 250,000 small customers — and the ir customers are looking for “outsourced IT” and consultative selling. CDW also procures from the large distributors, such as SYNNEX and Ingram Micro.

CDW effectively collects a spread on IT spending, which grows approximately high single digits each year, and with limited invested capital, they are able to compound EBIT, EPS, and cash flow faster than revenues over time.

In terms of varying perceptions, number one, CDW is a cloud and AI beneficiary. The market views them as a glorified laptop seller that is going to be left behind by AI spending. This thesis has actually popped up many times before, first from the shift from hardware to software, and then from on-prem to cloud. CDW has proven its ability to adapt and capture its fair share of software and cloud spending over time. CDW has twice the gross profit dollars from software services and warranties than they did in 2019 (when the stock was trading at these levels).

CDW's role is critical in the ecosystem; the presenter does not think they are losing share.

There is also a thesis that higher prices on hardware is going to hurt CDW. The presenter thinks this is neutral to positive, because CDW collects a spread on IT spending. If IT spending is higher, all else equal, CDW should have more gross profit dollars. They do not see IT budgets declining in absolute dollars. They think that, if anything, the budgets could be flat, and customers defer purchases until a later period, so CDW should benefit at some point. In terms of the pathway forward from here, The Street has them exiting 2026 growing gross profit dollars at approximately 1.5% year over year. The presenter thinks they do much better than that. CDW is really a coiled spring post-COVID. As everyone knows, workers spread out during the pandemic. They were working remotely. They needed firewalls, networking, laptops, phones, so there was a big hangover in terms of spending. That is starting to unwind, as people replace all that equipment. And you have AI, on-prem, data organization, and things like that occurring now.

CDW is also carrying a lot of headcount, because they were expecting that boom to continue, and it did not. They just kept those people on. So, if they do not get a recovery there, the presenter thinks management should pull those people out of the organization, and so you should get a profit recovery in any case.

The presenter thinks the stock is conservatively worth 15x $12 of 2027 EPS, which would be 30% upside. It is not unreasonable to think this is more like a high teens multiple on $13 of EPS, which would equate to 60%+ upside in approximately a year. The presenter does not think the management team here is amazing, in terms of walking investors off a cliff last year on expense guidance and things like that, but it is a solid business over time.

ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Akamai as a long.

This is a declining CDN business, a share loser in the maturing security market, but they have a compute business that represents upside optionality in AI inference at the edge play.

Right now, it is a 6% top-line grower that the presenter thinks can inflect to 10% plus in two-and-a-half years. But the market has since moved on from the OpenClaw hype. The real bull thesis is that they are building a compute business that is only 17% of mix today. That has a real attach rate component to the CDM and security business, with large incumbents and customers today, that the presenter thinks can CAGR at 50% for many years.

Right now, the presenter already sees enterprise AI demand in inference starting to inflect, with Anthropic and Codex. The presenter thinks that these two combined, the AI inference market is $30 billion this year, going to $150 billion in four to five years. All you need to underwrite is that the edge and low latency market TAM in AI inference is mid to high-single digits, and that Akamai can take mid-single digit share of those workloads. That is already a multi-billion-dollar opportunity that can help the compute business CAGR at 50% for a long time.

The presenter thinks there are already current use cases in large Fortune 500 companies that they have talked to in the financial services industry, that are exploring AI inference deployment closer to the edge. There are large card companies today that are using fraud detection use cases. The presenter believes that demonstrates that they can increase the current spend by 2x to 4x on Akamai and cloud and keep all the traffic within the same network of security and governance, not routing it out to hyperscalers, CDNs, or centralized compute data centers, in order to keep everything secure. Those test cases and POCs are already occurring today.

LLMs and AI agents' deployment requires a lot more than just sending signals to centralized regions and getting long-range inference results back. They require specialized small language models that a lot of enterprises are also already building today, and those use cases are real.

The presenter thinks it is easy to underwrite $9 of EPS in CY 2028. Right now, it trades at 12.5x PE (on next year). Using a 15x P/E on a $9.00 EPS in CY 2028 gets you to 20% upside.

However, with an EPS CAGR that is accelerating at 6%, and top line going at 10%, the presenter thinks you can argue for more multiple expansion. 20x P/E on this stock can get you 40% upside, discounting back.
