ideas.th: Market thinks Onto lost TSMC to KLA; Dragonfly 5 qualifying Apr-Jun wins back share at higher margins amid memory/leading-edge upcycle
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Onto Innovation as a long.

In terms of the business, Onto Innovation provides comprehensive process solutions across the semiconductor value chain, specializing in inspection, metrology, lithography and software. The machines are primarily used for error detection or inspection and measurement for metrology.

Before getting into the thesis, the presenter will give some background in terms of the stock's history. If you remember 12 to 14 months ago, Nvidia was suffering from yield issues as they started to ramp Blackwell. So, Nvidia went to TSMC – who gives them the wafers — and they said they needed help finding errors that were permissible but no longer are. The presenter believes TSMC then went to their inspection provider Onto and said, “H ey, we know this is not on the roadmap, we know you do not expect this, but we need a higher resolution to detect errors and we need it now.”

The presenter thinks Onto then tried to cobble something together very quickly, but ultimately, it was not expected, and so Onto did not have the machine. TSMC told Onto they were going to go to KLA — since they have higher resolution on the front end — and TSMC was going to use some of their machines temporarily on the back end where Onto operates.

They wanted Onto to take the time to develop the next generation machine that would ultimately work.

The headline that printed to the market was, “Onto losing share to KLA with TSMC, on the leading edge, and is an AI loser,” which is one of the most damning headlines you can get in semiconductors, and subsequently the stock got cut in half. Then there was the HBM digestion, so the stock suffered tremendously.

The thesis has a few points. First, the presenter believes the market is going to get the inverse of that headline. What Onto has done since then is, they have produced a new machine called Dragonfly 5, and Dragonfly 5 is passing all the specs to be able to meet all of TSMC’s requirements. The re are test wafers; it is passing on test wafers. There are production wafers; it is passing all the production wafers. In the presenter’s opinion, Onto effectively announced today that they shipped the machine to TSMC, so it is on the way to TSMC's facilities. And the optics, which is the hardest part of the machine, are now complete.

So, the presenter believes that the machine is going to TSMC and thinks it is going to qualify in and around the April to June time-frame. Management is saying they are going to win back half the share that they lost. The presenter believes that they are going to get the inverse of that headline, and that will be great for the multiple. Plus, that machine is significantly accretive to gross margins. KLA took the pricing umbrella up by approximately 30%+. Onto can now price closer to that point so, you get significant gross margin expansion on the incrementals for this new machine as well. That is point number one.

Second, memory and leading edge logic are going into dramatic up cycles. The world needs more chips, and this is clearly apparent across the board in terms of customers announcing more fab build outs. All the semi-cap players sound materially better today than they did two to three weeks ago, and better than they did two to three months ago. It is an up and to the right trajectory. So, they are all building more capacity. If you look at DRAM fundamentals, by charting out the number of GPUs and XPUs that will be built, and then the DRAM attached — you are going to need to see a very significant amount of additional DRAM that needs to come online. The world is dramatically undersupplied to the ASML pitch, along with other DRAM beneficiaries. It is not disclosed, but the presenter believes Onto’s business is roughly 40% memory, so, they are a significant beneficiary of this.

On the leading edge logic side, TSMC is a large customer. The presenter thinks the new machine is going to qualify. But even agnostic to the new machine, TSMC is also aggressively ramping as well on a very similar theme. There is a “bottoms up” arguments for it, the customer is asking for it, and there is even a geopolitical argument between the U.S. and Taiwan trade deal. That is essentially point number two: these industries are going into a significant inflection, and Onto is a big beneficiary in the 40% of their business that is exposed to memory, 20% exposed to foundry & leading edge logic.

Point three of the thesis is, you have additional call options that are interesting. On the valuation side, Onto is trading at 30x PE. Many semi-cap peers are trading north of 40x PE, whether it is NVMI, LAM, etc. It is one of the cheaper names in the space. The presenter believes that you will see multiple expansion as the narrative improves on the first two thesis points.

In terms of the setup, the presenter believes that they will beat on gross margins. In the presenter’s opinion, the company finally brought in a new CFO who is materially improved from the prior CFO. He brought gross margin discipline to his prior role, and the presenter thinks he is doing the same here. They are shifting capacity overseas, which is an immediate gross margin tailwind, because they are currently paying tariffs to import parts to the US to create machines. Those overhangs will be relieved as they move through this year. And you get additional call options as those factors play out.

The presenter is underwriting $10 of EPS in CY 2027. If it trades at 30x EPS at that point and they assert themselves as an AI beneficiary — again, it has traded north of 40x in the past – 30x that $10 would equate to 50% upside from current levels.

ideas.th: Identity numbers have troughed; renewal headwinds lapped, specialized sales force and governance/agent identity drive CRPO beats and re-acceleration
ideas.cat: Q4 CRPO beat; FY27 guide; $1B buyback
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Okta as a long.

At $94 per share, it has a $16.5 billion market cap, with $2 billion in net cash, and trades $200 million per day.

In terms of the business, it is a leading identity security platform, known mostly for workforce single sign-on and customer identification, but increasingly doing governance and securing all identities. Going forward, there is a call option on securing non-human agent identities.

The stock has been “in the penalty box” like the rest of the software sector but also due to some idiosyncratic dynamics coming out of the pandemic, with renewal cohorts, go-to-market disruptions, and a few other issues. But from here, the presenter thinks the setup is cleaner and easier to underwrite. In the presenter’s view, it looks like numbers have mostly troughed and the presenter thinks they have a positive revision cycle ahead. Renewal headwinds have lapped, the sales organization is now fully re-va mped, and specialization in go-to-market is working.

As the presenter mentioned, numbers are in a good place. CRPO is growing low teens.

Subscription revenue is currently modeled to grow high single digits, likely to inflect in CY 2026. Their new products in governance IGA are starting to contribute, and the presenter thinks they beat on CRPO in the current quarter with a slight guide ahead for FY 2027, with several hundred basis points of upside as the year unfolds.

The presenter’s checks and survey work are supportive. CIOs have consistently pointed to identity as a priority spend area, especially in the context of AI.

Additionally, the presenter believes the valuation is attractive. Okta stands out as one of the few companies where growth can re-accelerate. It trades anemically relative to the rest of their security and identity peers.

So why identity? It is less exposed to AI risk, and it should be a beneficiary of AI adoption.

At a high level, Okta secures humans logging into enterprise apps and customers logging into consumer apps, but going forward, non-human identities and AI agents will be acting autonomously across systems, and they provide security for all of that. A gents need their own identities, just-in-time access, governance, certification, and monitoring, as well as protection against privilege sprawl. This convergence trend across identity access, governance, and privilege access is something Okta is offering. It is still early, but the presenter thinks Okta has a right to win in this space. Touching quickly on their go-to-market strategy, execution looks better. The specialization of their sales force has seen higher win rates. Attrition is near cycle lows. They are moving a bit more upmarket (i.e. “land and expand”). The penetration is still relatively modest — 60% of Fortune 500 and 40% of Global 2000 — so the presenter believes there is upside there. They have new products in OIG (Identity Governance), which the presenter thinks is 10% penetrated and is a big part of the upsell.

Putting some numbers around it, the presenter thinks they see two to three points of CRPO upside in Q4. The FY 2027 guide is likely slightly ahead of the Street but ultimately will likely be in the low teens. The presenter thinks the stock can reach $130 over the next 12 months, which would equate to 5.5x revenue. The company recently announced a $1 billion-dollar buyback, which is supportive.

In terms of risk / reward, the presenter thinks the stock is $80 / $130. Numbers are finally set up for positive revisions. Identity is a desirable part of security. In summary, it is a beneficiary of AI and the valuation and technicals are supportive.

ideas.th: Holds 60% of Brazil adults but ~4% of profit pool; product expansion, open banking, Mexico/Colombia lending ramp and AI underwriting drive EPS
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Nubank as a long.

They are a digital bank focused on Latin America. Part one of the thesis is, if you were to go around the globe and map by three vectors, the size of GDP, the ROAs of incumbent banks — how profitable they are, how inefficient they are, and the markets that they are in — Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia — they would be some of the first markets you would want to go after with extremely compelling market opportunities.

Their core / home market is Brazil. They have approximately 60% share of the adult population as customers in Brazil. There is a ton of opportunity to close the gap, though, because when you map out the gross profit pools in Brazil for banking, they still only have approximately 4% of the gross profit pool. Sixty percent plus of the adult population is still growing users, but only 4% of the gross profit pool. Those two things will converge over time. Banking is a commodity. They have a much leaner cost structure. They pass it on to the consumer in the form of better yields on deposits, and lower yields on loans. By doing so, they pass along a lower cost structure. They are also a technology company with a better user experience. So, the presenter would argue, it is a better product at a lower cost.

Additionally, within Brazil, you have one of the most progressive central banks in the world that is really pushing for an open banking system. They are asking all the incumbent banks to connect to these centralized pipes, so that any banking app (with user consent), has the ability to share information and data. But not only that, an ability to port around and move around your deposits. A customer could go into the banking app, and Nubank, for instance, would be able to say to the customer that they know the customer has deposits earning 4% to 5% at Bradesco and offer to pay them something that is double that.

The presenter believes that Nubank has a better product at a lower cost. They will continue to narrow the gap between those two factors. The other important point is understanding why they only have 4% or 5% gross profit share so far. If you go product-by-product, product one that they launched was credit cards, product two was personal loans, and they are getting into payroll loans — they have reached high levels in terms of market share in every product that they launched first. In the presenter’s opinion, the reason that they do not have a higher percent of market share so far is that they simply have not gotten into most of the products that make up the gross profit pool so far.

Another key aspect of the story is their expansion markets outside of Brazil which are Mexico and Colombia. In aggregate, Mexico and Colombia are approximately the same size in terms of GDP as Brazil, with half the credit penetration (so, it should be a good greenfield story). In Mexico, there is also a banking oligopoly, but in fact it is even worse, because the Mexico based banks do not like to lend. In Mexico, they are perfectly content to operate where they pay nothing on deposits, and they park those deposits in risk-free securities.

Nubank is coming in and actually trying to build a credit model and lend and pay up for deposits. In Mexico, in the span of three or four years, they have gotten to over 10% of the population, but they only have 1% of the gross profit pool in those geographies. They are going to drag-and-drop a nd will likely have a similar outcome as in Brazil, the presenter thinks.

An important point to mention on Mexico is that when they came in, they led with deposits.

They made a big splash by essentially offering the risk-free rate in Mexico on deposits. They have aggregated a huge deposit base, but the balance sheet is incredibly inefficient. They have taken your deposits in at the risk-free rate, and they have parked those deposits in risk-free securities, earning effectively a 0% interest margin. But now you are starting to see them really ramp lending, because they figured out and cracked the code on underwriting.

If that happens in Mexico and in some of these expansion markets (given the excess capital this company has), in terms of getting to a similar level of mature profitability that Brazil has, this stock is not trading at 20x earnings, optically. It is trading at 13x. The presenter is highly confident of that, it is simply a matter of time.

The last piece to the thesis that the presenter thinks is interesting is at the beginning of 2025, they bought an AI research lab called Hyperplane. It is a financials-focused AI research lab, and they have been building, using transformer models, new supplementary models for underwriting. This is, to some extent, a little bit of a “black box” — since there is no way to fully validate it — but they have said a couple of things that stand out in the presenter’s view.

One, this is allowing them to use and leverage a lot of data that sits in the bank. For example, 80% of the data that sits in the bank is unstructured or semi-structured. They are now able to use a lot more information in underwriting the consumer.

And two, this is allowing them to experiment and iterate on models a lot more quickly. This is one of the few companies the presenter has seen that is actually — at least so far, it looks like — made a material change, and you are seeing it in the P&L already. The first product that they launched these new models for was for credit cards in Brazil. Since doing that, they have basically doubled the rate of credit expansion in that product. It is interesting because that is their most mature product, the product that should be the hardest to iterate on and improve, and you are already seeing a meaningful change there.

From what the presenter has heard from them, the presenter believes they have been testing similar models in other products in Brazil and similar products in Mexico. Whether you believe the AI story or not, the company is accelerating. The presenter thinks they will generate $1.30 of EPS in 2027. The stock should be able to hold the multiple at 20x. This would equate to a mid $20s target price for what the presenter describes is a great opportunity with a great management team.

ideas.th: Trades 1 SD below historical multiple; Azure miss was supply-driven, new capacity and $250B OpenAI commitment re-accelerate Azure to mid-40s%
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Microsoft as a long.

In terms of the setup, it feels like “catching a falling knife,” but the presenter thinks it is way too cheap at this valuation. The stock has meaningfully underperformed since the end of September. Using consensus NTM estimates, it trades one standard deviation below its historical average on both an earnings and EBITDA basis. On a relative multiple to the S&P, it is well below two standard deviations. It does not happen often historically, but it does happen from time to time, and when it does, it represents a good buying opportunity over the next 6 to 12 months.

On top of that, the presenter’s CY 2027 EPS is 7% higher than the consensus, with the delta mainly coming from Azure. It currently trades at 22x the presenter’s EPS estimate of $21.50, and the presenter thinks 30x — which is still a slight discount to the historical average — is more appropriate. That would imply a $645 price target by year end, which represents 37% upside from current levels.

So, why has the stock underperformed? The presenter thinks the first obvious reason is that software is in the dumps, and Microsoft is obviously the bellwether. Also, last quarter, earnings did underwhelm. The prior two quarters were in a very good beat-and-raise cadence that was reminiscent of 2021 and 2022. Then last quarter, both the Azure result and guide missed the bogeys, and that hurt the momentum for the stock.

And then there is the constant fears regarding a potential AI bubble, over-reliance on OpenAI, slowing enterprise adoption of AI, Gemini resurgence, and the higher CAPEX spend. What the presenter would say is, demand is strong. The reason why they missed last quarter was mainly supply-related. Management has highlighted many times — not just during the earnings call, but during the conference circuit — that demand is strong and it is broad-based. Again, the miss last Quarter was mainly due to supply constraints.

Commercial RPO actually hit $392 billion, which was up + 51% last quarter, which serves as an acceleration from the prior mid +30% growth rate. That does not even include the $250 billion commitment they got from OpenAI. Yes, CAPEX was again revised higher, but that is basically supporting the backlog that they have visibility on. Furthermore, they just increased prices on both Azure Cloud and M365 by approximately 6% to 10%. That took effect on November 1st, so that should help starting in the December quarter.

The presenter thinks most importantly, there is visibility into supply coming online. It is not just third parties like Coreweave, but also their own first-party Fairwater facilities in Wisconsin and in Atlanta. That should hit most likely in the first half of this year, and from there, you should see almost immediate revenue upside. Net of that, the presenter thinks Azure re-accelerates into the mid 40% range by CY 2027.

Simply looking at the $250 billion OpenAI commitment, if you assume it is an eight-year commitment, that is essentially $30 billion per year off a $90 billion Azure base. The presenter is not assuming that all comes in this year, but it is easy to imagine that they could accelerate by 7 to 10 points just on that. ideas.th: PC peripheral sales fall with memory-driven PC weakness; tariff price hikes failing vs Chinese rivals and OEM bundling; AI shrinks knowledge-worker seats
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Logitech as a short.

The company makes PC peripherals such as keyboards, headsets, video conferencing equipment, and accessories. The business is approximately 60% consumer and 40% enterprise. This is a compelling short for a few reasons. First, the company's sales have a high correlation with PC sales. Particularly in consumer and gaming, the presenter believes PC sales are in a challenged place next year due to memory pricing and availability. While the industry should be down at least high single digits, the specific exposures that matter most to Logitech should be down at least 10%, and that is very problematic for their top line.

Second, the company's strategy to combat the incremental cost brought on by tariffs — both directly, in terms of the 10% of the US business they plan to serve out of China, and indirectly, as they shift to higher cost areas in Asia and Mexico — is to increase price. The presenter believes that their strategy is already failing, and they are folding on price, which the presenter believes you can verify looking at the alternative data.

The presenter thinks this is the case because; 1) they compete with lower-end gaming providers in China who are undercutting them on price. 2) Large PC OEMs are trying to make up for lost margin in PC with peripherals. Dell, HPQ, and others have made public comments about attacking the peripheral space via bundling, which bodes poorly for Logitech, and consumer and enterprise budgets are already stretched with higher PC ASPs, which leaves less room for the peripheral budget.

Finally, Logitech is a long-term AI loser. Knowledge worker seats are compressing (simply look at any SaaS stock). Logitech's enterprise business, as a result, should have worse refresh cycles through time, ultimately derating the stock through the cycle.

The Street thinks the company can grow 5% in FY 2027 (ending in March). The presenter thinks it declines approximately 5% and earns $4.50 EPS in FY 2027. The stock trades with a mid-teens multiple when it is not growing, so at 15x, this implies a price target of $67.50, which is approximately 30% below current levels.

This business has already hit an inflection point on net adds, and now for the first time since they have gone public, they are likely going to see sales and marketing leverage, which is pretty unique. Now investors are looking at a high single digit / low double digit revenue grower for the next several years, with high 20%s EBITDA growth during that period.

Management is finally talking about marketing efficiencies going forward, and in the presenter’s view, that makes sense. They are past the COVID hangover. The pet market is now effectively an oligopoly controlled by Chewy, Amazon, and Walmart. All the brick-and-mortar players are struggling in a major way. Important to note, cohort trends have stabilized. Many customers are now in the ir second year or more in terms of their lifetime activation curve. And when that occurs, your churn typically goes down dramatically. It makes it a lot easier for the incremental gross adds to retain and improve your net adds.

And AI has made marketing channels much more efficient. It is just much easier to target and find those specific customers at their vulnerable points now than it had been in the past.

From the presenter’s perspective, if you put a 20x to 25x multiple on their 2028 free cash flow and discount it back, the presenter thinks the stock could be worth $60 in a year's time. In terms of downside, the presenter thinks there is only $10 to the downside.

In the presenter’s downside scenario, they think there is only 10% downside from here. It assumes net adds slow to 300k in 2026, well below the 700k annualized rate they did in 2H25, amidst tough comps. If the presenter is entirely wrong, you will see incremental gross margin and fulfillment leverage come off and you put an 11-12x multiple on out year 2028 EBITDA and discount it back using 15x 2028 FCF, would only equate to 10% downside from current levels.

The presenter thinks the risk/reward is $10 / $80 for a company that is experiencing a business model shift.

ideas.th: Litho monopoly underappreciated as DRAM play; rising litho intensity at TSMC next node plus less-efficient Intel/Samsung foundry demand
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss ASML as a long.

ASML produces lithography equipment that essentially prints designs on semiconductors.

They are effectively a monopoly in the high-end portion of this market. They have 90% share of the “premium” portion of the market, such as immersion DUV (Deep Ultraviolet) tools.

As much as investors love Micron and the DRAM companies at the moment, they should remember that they need tools to install to continue growing capacity to support all of this AI ramp over time. ASML has historically not been viewed as a DRAM player, but it has actually grown to be 35% to 40% of the business, in the presenter’s opinion. The presenter thinks there is upside to that going forward.

Important to note, as we are now in a more advanced DRAM phase, the insertion of the most premium tools, where they have 100% market share, is going to be expanding. Some investors are worried that there are going to be alternative solutions that do not require as much intensity of lithography tools. But the presenter does not see that happening until 2029 at the earliest, given their understanding of their customer’s desires.

In addition to that, if you look at what TSMC is doing, they are starting to insert more layers of that same ultra-high-end tool that ASML has a monopoly in. And that starts with the upcoming node, and then it continues to expand from there, after they skipped growing lithography intensity in the last generation, which is one of the reasons why ASML is cheaper and has not re-rated to the same degree as some of the other semiconductor capital equipment companies.

Beyond TSMC, Intel is becoming viewed as a real potential alternative to TSMC — even if it is just because TSMC has no capacity, which is the reason the presenter thinks they are getting business. But that company is much less efficient with tools, and the presenter thinks they have been able to quantify specifically for lithography that they need more equipment than TSMC needs. So as a proportion of revenue for the industry, ASML will outgrow the foundry business.

And Samsung is also starting to pick up business (i.e. based on the presenter’s work, they believe Qualcomm is moving business to Samsung). That company is even less efficient than Intel is in terms of lithography.

In summary, this company is going to massively outgrow the markets that they serve, and they are all being driven by AI and eventually edge compute as well. It is less of a bet, specifically, on the data center itself. In terms of valuation, the presenter thinks ASML earns mid to low $40s EPS in CY 2027 and applying a 40x multiple would equate to approximately 35% upside in the stock from current levels.

ideas.th: Connector oligopolist and NVIDIA connector-of-choice; AI DC revenue to ~$8B, non-AI cyclical recovery and M&A drive 30%+ EPS growth
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Amphenol as a long.

The presenter is constructive on the AI infrastructure theme and the way they are playing it is through Amphenol. The presenter would describe Amphenol as an industrial tech company now, but data center is becoming approximately 25% of the business in 2026.

In terms of the business, Amphenol produces electronic and fiber optic connectors. For context, they make 15% to 20% of all the connectors in the world. It has been an amazing oligopoly, with three companies gaining share against the rest for 30 years, and they will likely continue to do so, because they are very low value but obviously mission critical products and you typically do not switch vendors.

This company is one of the best long-term compounders that has grown earnings into high teens over the last 20 to 30 years. Why it has been interesting over the last couple years, and why the presenter thinks it will remain so, is t hreefold.

The presenter thinks first, in AI, they have a very R&D-heavy organization (they have 4,000 engineers). From talking to formers, channel partners, and customers, the presenter believes that it is the only company in the space that will invest in R&D dollars to create markets. So, the same language as NVIDIA, creating new markets, versus other companies who wait for established markets to come to them. They invested with NVIDIA to be the “connector of choice” for their systems and they have clearly benefited from that. AI revenue has gone from zero to exiting this year at approximately $5 billion. The presenter thinks it should be north of $8 billion in CY 2026. With NVIDIA on an annual cadence, there is no time for a second player to properly catch up, so, Amphenol should maintain above 50% market share in the core connectors that they produce.

The controversy right now is how the architecture will change, and whether that takes out copper. The presenter believes that at least for the next two generations, the copper cables might go away, but the conductor that they produce is not going away. In the presenter’s view, Jensen Huang essentially confirmed that on stage at CES a few days ago. So, they are actually even denser in the new systems than the old ones, so, the content keeps going up.

The presenter assumes the content stays flat, which is a fairly conservative assumption, because they know that you are connecting more GPUs to more GPUs, so the content should be going up. Even then, the presenter is underwriting ~$8 billion of AI data center revenue this year.

The second vector is non-AI related. For background, the macro has been fine but not great in terms of the industrial economy. Over the last six months, most companies the presenter follows, specifically the analog semiconductor companies are solidly comping positive numbers now. The presenter thinks there is a macro-cyclical recovery. They are indexed to all of that, and they are indexed to the military boom that is occurring. So, if you believe that there is a non-AI recovery after a negative year, the presenter thinks it could at least be 6% to 7% growth. They look at an ADI that trades at 30x, and that is sort of the top line that investors look at.

You can combine both of those, and then you add a third vector, which is M&A. They are exceptional at doing M&A, mostly tuck-in deals throughout their history. They have bought more than 100 companies. But it is worth highlighting that they bought a fiber company from a company that was going bankrupt early last year. Th at deal closed just a few days ago. The presenter estimates the company paid 12x EBIT for a company growing 50%. In the presenter’s view, this essentially future proofs them as they become more optical in fiber and in AI data centers.

Combining all of that together, the presenter assumes earnings growth of 45% this year, and north of 30% growth over the next three years. They assume GAAP EPS of $7.30 in CY 2028, and they are using a 30x GAAP P/E multiple. For context, the pre-AI multiple was 28x, so a 30x multiple is not excessive in their view. ADI and other analog semi companies with a teens EPS growth rate are trading at that multiple. The presenter gets to a mid to high-20% s IRR.

In summary, the presenter thinks there are so many ways to win, and they are comfortable knowing that if there are architecture changes, Amphenol is generally fine. Additionally, there is a real non-AI business, a great management team, and an M&A engine that continues to compound through cycle.

ideas.th: Market sees BNPL as infrequent big-ticket; Affirm Card becomes everyday payment network (~30% of GMV by FY28), lifting EBITDA well above Street
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Affirm as a long.

Affirm is a leading U.S. “buy now, pay later” platform and flexible payment network serving 24 million active consumers and 420,000 merchant partners across a range of verticals. The company's core offering is installment-based, consumer financing over four-week to 60-month terms, underwritten using proprietary risk models and real-time transaction-level decision-making.

Affirm has also expanded their offering with the Affirm card, better positioning the platform within the broader financial ecosystem. Revenue is generated through merchant discount rates, interest income on longer duration loans, and network-driven engagement. Affirm has consistently compounded GMV in the 30%+ range for several years, taking share in the BNPL space and within e-commerce more broadly. BNPL has now penetrated high single-digit share in the $1.2 trillion U.S. e-commerce market, with a massive opportunity in point of sale, where BNPL (broadly speaking) currently has 1% share in North America. There are also massive opportunities in both international and B2B. As an example of the international opportunity, geographies like Australia have approximately 15% BNPL penetration. The presenter believes that there will be other countries with propensity to use BNPL, as well as further room to expand in the US.

The presenter thinks Affirm is being mispriced because the market views BNPL as an infrequent, big ticket product. The Affirm debit card is quietly turning into an everyday merchant-agnostic payment network, driving higher usage frequency in GMV, improving underwriting and margins, and expanding the opportunity well beyond current expectations. The presenter thinks the market has misread the enormous potential of the card, which will contribute approximately 30% of GMV by FY 2028. The presenter thinks you will see active card consumers nearly tripling to approximately 7.5 million by Q4 FY 2028, which equates to a ~20% attach rate (using the presenter’s numbers) and is well within management’s long-term target of 20 million active card consumers. The presenter also thinks annual spend per consumer will reach ~$4,000 by Q4 FY 2028, which is roughly a double versus current levels.

The presenter thinks the Affirm card directly addresses core issues of traditional credit cards, which are revolving balances, compounding interest, penalty fees, and opaque terms, and offers a fundamentally better mousetrap for near-prime and prime consumers. The presenter thinks as the impact of the Affirm card becomes more tangible, they see 50% upside to the current share price based on a 15x multiple applied to $2.25 billion of EBITDA (which is well ahead of Street estimates of $1.8 billion of EBITDA in FY 2028). Discounted back, it equates to approximately a low 20 s EPS multiple using the presenter’s FY 2028 estimates.

ideas.th: Industrial recovery plus ATE/defense secular mix, comms transceiver ramp and price increases drive EPS to $11/$13+, above Street
ideas.pitch:
The presenter would like to discuss Analog Devices as a long.

ADI is a broad-based semiconductor supplier (industrial is ~50% of their sales, auto ~25%, and the remainder split evenly between the communications and consumer end markets). In industrial, Street annual estimates suggest the industrial business will grow slightly above seasonal throughout the year, though the presenter expects additional upside.

When you look at ADI's business mix in industrial, it has shifted more towards secular opportunities, and an AI-focused ATE segment in aerospace and defense. Over the years, these two businesses are now more than a third of industrial, versus less than a quarter a few years ago. ADI has also gained share in the ATE business, exceeding 60% today versus less than 50% a few years ago. On the defense side, you have strengthening budgets globally, and other unique drivers like expanding LEO programs that should help sustain the defense strength moving forward.

Outside of the secular trends inflecting, ADI is beginning to accelerate sequentially in annual growth in their more cyclical markets, which should further support well above seasonal growth. This lends support to the expected 10% to 30% price increases that could occur on parts, likely more than offsetting any inflationary cost pressures.

ADI's communication business could also see upside. Sixty percent of the segment is related to wireline applications. Specifically, ADI benefits from accelerating transceiver deployments, with high-speed shipments potentially in line to more than double year-over-year. ADI is also making inroads in the vertical power market. Even on the wireless side, the inventory overhang appears to be largely cleared, which should abate as a headwind moving forward. The Street’s forecast of low double-digit, million-dollar growth quarter-over-quarter (beyond the January quarter) seems conservative.

Beyond the two growth segments, the presenter believes that the automotive estimates are set conservatively — only modestly above SA AR — which should account for potential industry digestion or potential customer digestion at a large auto OEM. If this customer remains resilient, this could present further upside for ADI, which has historically grown its auto business 10 points or more above SA AR. The combination of the industrial communication outperformance should also provide a mix benefit, which should provide gross margin expansion.

Putting it all together, the presenter thinks ADI can generate $11 in EPS this fiscal year and more than $13 in EPS the following fiscal year. Using a mid to high-20s multiple — which is below the peak but in between the median peak — the presenter believes the stock can trade up to $360 pretty easily. And then if the multiple gets back to that 30x and above range, you can start approaching $400. For reference, the stock is currently trading at $300. The risk-reward is still more than 2:1, which is attractive in the presenter’s view.
